stories.headline: NBA offseason recap, early 2026-27 season previews by team
stories.summary: We're looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the regular season by rolling out one team profile each weekday through Sept. 18.
stories.body:
After an eventful July full of big trades, intriguing signings and the game's biggest star shocking everyone by heading East, the NBA offseason is nearly complete. And with the regular-season schedule now out, it's time to start thinking about the 2026-27 season.

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for every team.

Check out the rollout schedule below, with stories added daily:

Quick links:

Free agency buzz | FA grades | Trade grades

Transactions | Schedule | More NBA coverage

Southeast Division

Miami Heat: Aug. 31
Key additions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Klay Thompson, Bobby Portis, Tim Hardaway Jr., Nick Richards

Key retentions: Andrew Wiggins, Simone Fontecchio

Key subtractions: Tyler Herro, Norman Powell, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis

Heat president Pat Riley landed the superstar he'd been searching for since LeBron James left Miami in 2016. Antetokounmpo is in the fold, and Miami is ready to contend for another title with the two-time MVP. Antetokounmpo is just as motivated to win his second title and remind everyone that he can be the best player in the league.

In the trade, the Heat gave up key players such as Herro, Ware and Jaquez and did not bring back Powell in free agency. They landed Thompson to a two-year, $13 million deal after the four-time champion sharpshooter worked out a buyout with the Dallas Mavericks. Miami also added Portis and Hardaway, but the team is still looking to bolster the roster around Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Heat offseason recap/season preview

Washington Wizards: Sept. 1
Key additions: AJ Dybantsa, Khris Middleton, Deandre Ayton, Tre Mann

Key subtractions: Cam Whitmore, D'Angelo Russell, Jaden Hardy

Key retentions: Trae Young

The Wizards got their jump on this pivotal offseason by acquiring Trae Young and Anthony Davis last season in trades.

Those were their two big moves and then came the big prize for losing 65 games last season - winning the lottery and drafting AJ Dybantsa with the first overall pick.

Ready to start winning games this season after losing 60 or more games in each of the past three years, Washington gave Young a four-year, $212 million contract. The Wizards added veterans like Khris Middleton and Deandre Ayton to bolster the depth behind their young core featuring the likes of Dybantsa, Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George, Tre Johnson and Will Riley. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Wizards offseason recap/season preview

Charlotte Hornets: Sept. 2
Key additions: F Naz Reid, G Grayson Allen, G Dennis Schroder, F Royce O'Neale, F Dorian Finney-Smith

Key retentions: G Coby White

Key subtractions: G LaMelo Ball, F Miles Bridges, G Josh Green, G Tre Mann

After enjoying their best season in a decade, the Hornets sharply changed course with the surprising decision to trade Ball, their franchise guard, to the Timberwolves.

Given that Ball was a borderline All-Star on a max contract, Charlotte opted for a "Moneyball" approach in hopes of avoiding the perpetual mediocrity that tripped up Trae Young's Atlanta Hawks in the recent past.

With Ball and starting forward Miles Bridges moved in separate deals aimed at collecting future draft assets and improving its cap flexibility, Charlotte is now the only team that doesn't have a single player on the books for at least $25 million next season. -- Ben Golliver

Read the full Hornets offseason recap/season preview

Atlanta Hawks: Sept. 3
Key additions: Luguentz Dort, Aaron Wiggins, Kingston Flemings, Devin Carter, Ryan Nembhard, Zuby Ejiofor, Henri Veesaar

Key retentions: CJ McCollum, Jock Landale

Key subtractions: Zaccharie Risacher, Jonathan Kuminga, Gabe Vincent, Keaton Wallace

Atlanta continued to move forward from the Trae Young trade last season by being opportunistic this offseason.

The Hawks acquired Dort and Wiggins in separate trades from the Oklahoma City Thunder to add more help around emerging star Jalen Johnson. The Hawks also kept McCollum on a one-year, $21 million deal and drafted Flemings eighth overall.

Atlanta is loaded with young wings looking to take a step forward under Quin Snyder like Nickeil Alexander-Walker did last season in winning Most Improved Player. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Hawks offseason recap/season preview

Orlando Magic: Sept. 4
Key additions: C Nikola Vucevic, G Izaiyah Nelson

Key subtractions: F Moritz Wagner, G Jett Howard

Key retentions: F Jonathan Isaac, G Jevon Carter

The Magic's biggest move this offseason was hiring Sean Sweeney to replace Jamahl Mosley.

Orlando also brought Nikola Vucevic back on a one-year, $3.9 million deal since trading him in 2021 and will use his ability to score and shoot to space the floor for Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner and Desmond Bane.

The Magic blew a 3-1 lead over top-seeded Detroit in the first round of the playoffs after Wagner went down due to injury and were in desperate need of someone who can get easier baskets and make outside shots. Vucevic should help. Moe Wagner departed for Brooklyn via free agency, separating Franz from his brother for the first time in his pro career. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Magic offseason recap/season preview

Pacific Division

Los Angeles Lakers: Aug. 24
Key additions: C Walker Kessler, F Sandro Mamukelashvili, G Quentin Grimes, G Collin Sexton, F Kevon Looney, F Matisse Thybulle, G Cameron Carr

Key retentions: G Austin Reaves

Key subtractions: F LeBron James, C Deandre Ayton, G Marcus Smart, F Rui Hachimura, G Luke Kennard, C Jaxson Hayes

James informed the Lakers he would not be returning for next season on June 30. Two days later, the team transformed the roster, with Doncic squarely as the focal point.

The biggest addition -- literally and figuratively -- is 7-foot-2 center Kessler, acquired in a sign-and-trade deal with the Utah Jazz. L.A. sent two unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033 and pick swaps in 2028 and 2030, not to mention a four-year, $130 million contract, to acquire him.

Mamukelashvili, Grimes, Sexton, Looney and Thybulle also signed with the Lakers, and free agent Ziaire Williams and first-round pick Carr bolster the team's young prospect pool of Adou Thiero, Bronny James and Dalton Knecht.

The most important move, though, came when Reaves, coming off a career season in which he averaged 23.3 points, 4.7 rebounds and 5.5 assists per game, signed a four-year, $180 million extension.

When the dust settled, it was a dramatic roster overhaul in what could prove to be one of the most consequential summers in franchise history, with the team also being sold for the second time in 14 months, this time to venture capitalist Josh Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger, who bought the Lakers from Mark Walter at a $12.5 billion valuation. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Lakers offseason recap/season preview

LA Clippers: Aug. 25
Key additions: Rui Hachimura, Keaton Wagler, Brandon Ingram (TBD), Gradey Dick (TBD)

Key retentions: Kobe Sanders, Bradley Beal

Key subtractions: Kawhi Leonard (TBD), Nicolas Batum, Bogdan Bogdanovic, John Collins

What started as a reconfiguration at the trade deadline -- acquiring Darius Garland from Cleveland for James Harden and Bennedict Mathurin from Indiana for Ivica Zubac -- turned into a complete overhaul this summer after the Clippers let Bogdan Bogdanovic, Nicolas Batum and John Collins walk.

Their biggest move, however, was trading Leonard to the Toronto Raptors for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick and draft picks, but that deal is in limbo pending the investigation into alleged salary cap circumvention by the team relating to Leonard's Aspiration endorsement deal.

In the meantime, LA added Illinois guard Wagler with the No. 5 pick in the draft and signed Hachimura away from the crosstown Lakers with a two-year, $28 million deal. And in a surprise move, Bradley Beal -- after declining his $5.6 million contract option for next season in June to test free agency -- ended up re-signing on a two-year, $13.2 million deal in mid-August to stay with the Clippers. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Clippers offseason recap/season preview

Golden State Warriors: Aug. 26
Key additions: Yaxel Lendeborg, Brandon Williams, Georges Niang

Key subtractions: Quinten Post, Pat Spencer

Key retentions: Draymond Green, Al Horford, Kristaps Porzingis, Gary Payton II, De'Anthony Melton

The Warriors opted for flexibility and stability over a larger shake-up around Curry. Their much-publicized recruitment of James never gained much traction.

They brought back their veteran frontcourt trio (Green, Horford, Porzingis), but kept them all on short-term maneuverable contracts. They opted for the fit of Melton over a pursuit of scoring guard Anfernee Simons. Their big addition is Lendeborg, the 23-year-old rookie wing who they will rely upon to be a high-minute, high-impact rotation player immediately.

In the bigger picture, they protected their draft pick cupboard and lined up their books to have an ocean of cap space as they peer a bit deeper into the future while their core ages. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Warriors offseason recap/season preview

Phoenix Suns: Aug. 27
Key additions: F Miles Bridges, F Koa Peat, G Luke Kennard

Key subtractions: G Grayson Allen, F Royce O'Neale

Key retentions: F Dillon Brooks, G Collin Gillespie, C Mark Williams, G Jordan Goodwin

Phoenix followed up its surprising season with a series of moves to mostly keep its team intact, with some adjustments around the margins.

The Suns re-signed Gillespie (four years, $48 million), Williams (three years, $38 million), Goodwin (three years, $19 million) and Brooks (three years, $73 million) to new deals and made a major splash by trading Allen and O'Neale to the Charlotte Hornets for Bridges. And despite not having a pick until No. 47 in the second round of the 2026 draft, Phoenix was able to acquire Arizona player Peat -- who averaged 14.1 points on 52.8% shooting as a freshman for the Wildcats and was key to their Final Four run. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Suns offseason recap/season preview

Sacramento Kings: Aug. 28
Key additions: G Darius Acuff Jr., F Alex Karaban, G Emanuel Sharp

Key subtractions: G DeMar DeRozan, G Russell Westbrook

Key retentions: F Precious Achiuwa

Perry, currently in the organization's power seat, is continuing a steady transition toward the younger core he has drafted. Arkansas guard and No. 7 pick Acuff is the spotlight name on a roster populated with six players in their first two NBA seasons.

But they still have notable high-minute holdovers from the past regime, including Murray, Malik Monk, LaVine and Sabonis. Of those four, Murray appears the most locked-in as a stable member of the team's long-term vision. Perry explored trades for Monk, LaVine and Sabonis over the past year, but didn't value the proposed returns, and the three are expected to open the season in Sacramento. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Kings offseason recap/season preview

Northwest Division

Portland Trail Blazers: Aug. 17
Key additions: G Ja Morant, F Jeremy Sochan

Key retentions: C Robert Williams III

Key subtractions: F Jerami Grant, F Kris Murray, G Matisse Thybulle

Sadly, the Blazers made far more noise this offseason with their off-court business dealings than anything they did with their roster. New owner Tom Dundon's aggressive cost-cutting measures and ongoing fight for arena financing have distracted from the progress that Portland made on the court last season, when it reached the playoffs for the first time since 2021.

Although the Blazers were the only team that sat out June's draft by not making a pick, they will add two high-profile guards to a rotation that otherwise looks very similar to last season. Lillard, a franchise icon, is back from an Achilles tendon injury that sidelined him for the entire 2025-26 campaign, and Morant, a two-time All-Star, arrived in a trade that sent Grant and Murray to the Memphis Grizzlies. -- Ben Golliver

Read the full Blazers offseason recap/season preview

Utah Jazz: Aug. 18
Key additions: G Darryn Peterson, C Jaxson Hayes, G Josh Okogie

Key retentions: C Jusuf Nurkic

Key subtractions: C Walker Kessler

The Jazz finally got some lottery luck, landing at No. 2 and taking Peterson, a gifted guard who has the potential to emerge as the face of the franchise. The hope was that Peterson would be the final major piece in Utah's rebuild, but that plan featured Kessler as the team's long-term starting center. Instead, the Jazz agreed to a sign-and-trade deal that sent Kessler to the Lakers in exchange for a pair of future first-round picks and two swaps.

The return was widely considered to be great value for Utah, particularly after Kessler's deal (four years, $130 million) pushed beyond the Jazz's comfort zone, but there is now a glaring need in the starting lineup alongside Jackson and Lauri Markkanen in the frontcourt. -- Tim MacMahon

Read the full Jazz offseason recap/season preview

Minnesota Timberwolves: Aug. 19
Key additions: G LaMelo Ball, G Josh Green, G Isaiah Evans

Key subtractions: F Julius Randle, C Naz Reid

Key retentions: G Ayo Dosunmu, G Bones Hyland, G Jaylen Clark

Wolves president of basketball operations Tim Connelly continued to show his aggression, orchestrating a four-team trade with the Brooklyn Nets, Chicago Bulls and Charlotte Hornets that sent out three-time All-Star Randle and the 2023-24 Sixth Man of the Year, Reid, and a future first-round pick to bring in the talented -- but polarizing -- Ball.

That move followed Connelly inking 6-foot-4 guard Dosunmu to a five-year, $112 million extension in June, following his acquisition at the deadline.

Minnesota also re-signed wing Clark and guard Hyland and acquired the 6-foot-6 Evans out of Duke with the No. 33 pick in the draft.

Coach Chris Finch also lost his top lieutenant on the bench, Micah Nori, who left to coach the Portland Trail Blazers. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Timberwolves offseason recap/season preview

Oklahoma City Thunder: Aug. 20
Key additions: C Aday Mara, G Bennett Stirtz

Key retentions: G Kenrich Williams, C Isaiah Hartenstein

Key subtractions: G Isaiah Joe, G Aaron Wiggins, G Luguentz Dort

The extensions for both Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren triggered in July, leading to a trio of financially motivated trades to slash the tax bill and cost-control the current roster.

They sent Isaiah Joe to Detroit and traded Aaron Wiggins and Lu Dort to Atlanta in separate moves, eroding their depth.

General manager Sam Presti made clear in an interview with The Oklahoman that the impression he's been given from ownership is "the savings generated this summer, and from being out of the tax the last several years, will be re-allocated to future teams."

That would mean extra breathing room to eventually extend core young players such as Cason Wallace and Ajay Mitchell. Wallace, the likely replacement starter for Dort, is extension eligible off his rookie contract into October. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Thunder offseason recap/season preview

Denver Nuggets: Aug. 21
Key additions: Marvin Bagley III, Lonnie Walker IV

Key retentions: Spencer Jones, Tyus Jones

Key subtractions: Watson, Tim Hardaway Jr., Jonas Valanciunas

Finding a resolution to Watson's restricted free agency was Denver's most important piece of summer business.

Watson is a draft success story, rising from the 30th overall pick into one of the league's more intriguing young two-way wings. But retaining the 23-year-old would have been expensive -- via either a sky-high luxury tax bill or a salary-slashing move to get off an important veteran and generate more breathing room for a new deal.

After Wednesday's deal to send Watson to Cleveland, Denver's front office can shift its attention to escaping the salary cap's second apron. The Nuggets are currently the league's only team above it. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Nuggets offseason recap/season preview

Southwest Division

Memphis Grizzlies: Aug. 14
Key additions: F Cameron Boozer, G D'Angelo Russell, F Isaiah Stewart, F Jerami Grant, F Kris Murray, C Quinten Post

Key retentions: None

Key subtractions: G Ja Morant, F Santi Aldama

Memphis finally traded Ja Morant, turning the last page from an ultimately disappointing chapter in franchise history, and already has his replacement as the face of the franchise in place: No. 3 pick Cameron Boozer. GM Zach Kleiman has overhauled the roster in the past few transaction cycles, acquiring four first-round picks when he traded Desmond Bane, a few more when he dealt Jaren Jackson Jr. and none for Morant, whose departure signaled a fresh start for the Grizzlies and him.

Memphis is in a full-blown youth movement, as 21-year-old forward GG Jackson is now the longest-tenured player on the roster. The Grizzlies say they believe they have a long-term foundation in place with their last few lottery picks: center Zach Edey, small forward Cedric Coward and power forward Boozer. -- Tim MacMahon

Read the full Grizzlies offseason recap/season preview

New Orleans Pelicans: Aug. 13
Key additions: None

Key retentions: C DeAndre Jordan

Key subtractions: F Kevon Looney

Despite capturing a combined 47 wins over the last two seasons under executive vice president Joe Dumars and general manager Troy Weaver, the Pelicans clearly believe that internal growth is the best path forward. Perhaps that justifies a near-silent summer in which the hiring of new coach Jamahl Mosley turned out to be the team's most notable move. Mosley becomes New Orleans' third coach since Dumars took the helm in April 2025. In addition to drafting Jaron Pierre Jr. in the second round, New Orleans signed just two new players over the summer in Kobe Bufkin and Hunter Dickinson, while bringing back 14 of the 15 players from last season's squad. -- Michael C. Wright

Read the full Pelicans offseason recap/season preview

Dallas Mavericks: Aug. 12
Key additions: F Morez Johnson Jr., F Zaccharie Risacher

Key retentions: Moussa Cisse

Key subtractions: Khris Middleton, Ryan Nembhard

The major changes made by the Mavericks this offseason were in the managerial and coaching ranks. After a seasonlong search, team governor Patrick Dumont hired Masai Ujiri to run the franchise's basketball operations, bringing the architect of the Toronto Raptors' 2019 title team to Dallas. Ujiri decided to part ways with coach Jason Kidd and recruited Dusty May, fresh off an NCAA title with Michigan, to replace him.

Johnson, who played for May at Michigan before the Mavs selected him with the No. 9 pick in the draft, is the headliner of the additions to the roster. Dallas added three potential immediate contributors in a six-team deal, acquiring former Grizzlies forward Santi Aldama, ex-Pistons guard Marcus Sasser and EuroLeague veteran Tarik Biberovic. The franchise also landed former No. 1 pick as part of the trade that sent Luguentz Dort from the Oklahoma City Thunder to the Atlanta Hawks. -- MacMahon

Read the full Mavericks offseason recap/season preview

Houston Rockets: Aug. 11
Key additions: G Marcus Smart, G Bogdan Bogdanovic

Key retentions: F Tari Eason

Key subtractions: F Dorian Finney-Smith, G Josh Okogie

After suffering a first-round postseason exit for the second consecutive season, the Rockets resisted the temptation to jump into the Giannis Antetokounmpo sweepstakes after adding former MVP Durant last summer. General manager Rafael Stone and coach Ime Udoka will instead lean on growth from the team's collection of young talent acquired in recent years, not to mention the continuity that comes with those players developing together over multiple seasons.

Houston signed Tari Eason to a five-year, $81.5 million extension over the summer. But outside of that, the Rockets focused on bolstering depth by bringing aboard veterans Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanovic. The club also brought in renowned shooting coach Chip Engelland from Oklahoma City. Engelland spent more than a decade with the San Antonio Spurs, winning two titles. -- Wright

Read the full Rockets offseason recap/season preview

San Antonio Spurs: Aug. 10
Key additions: F Tobias Harris

Key retentions: F Harrison Barnes

Key subtractions: None

San Antonio's surprising run to the NBA Finals never obscured its long-term vision for building a sustainable competitor around Victor Wembanyama. Clearly, the Frenchman views the future similarly, considering he signed a 25% max extension worth $252 million instead of the available 30% supermax escalators that would've rocketed the contract to $303 million.

Wembanyama did it to keep San Antonio's talented young core together for as long as possible, with added flexibility to acquire needed supporting players. The Spurs grabbed one of those in free agency in Harris, an experienced, reliable scorer who adds size (6-foot-8, 226 pounds) and physicality on defense while bolstering frontcourt depth in the draft. -- Wright

stories.headline: 2027 NFL draft: Kiper's early predictions on top prospects
stories.summary: Jadan Baugh as the RB1? Five first-round quarterbacks? Safeties and tight ends galore? Mel Kiper Jr. makes predictions for the 2027 NFL draft class.
stories.body:
Week 1 of the 2026 college football season is here, and I can't wait to spend every Saturday watching top prospects for the 2027 NFL draft class. It's an exciting group of players, starting with the quarterbacks.

I don't have a Big Board quite yet -- I like to see a few weeks' worth of games before I roll that out -- and I won't put together an official mock draft for a while. But I do like to make some way-too-early predictions before the season really ramps up (though Week 0 brought some fun, too). Things will certainly change; I had Clemson with four first-round picks in this space last August, and that didn't quite play out. But it's still good to map out how the draft landscape looks roughly eight months out.

How many QBs will go on Day 1? Which schools could take over the draft? Which position could be sneaky deep? And who could emerge from the FCS ranks? Here are 10 predictions for the 2027 draft -- plus my picks for the College Football Playoff and Super Bowl champions as an added bonus.

1. There will be at least five first-round quarterbacks.
Every summer, we hype the QB class. We talk about how multiple NFL teams will be able to find legit franchise passers in Round 1 the following April. It was the same case heading into the 2025 season. Sometimes the quarterback group lives up to all that hype, but oftentimes a few of the signal-callers don't take the projected step forward, opt to return to school or just fall flat.

The 2026 group fizzled, but the excitement around the 2027 class seems real. That's at least in part because a handful of the quarterbacks we thought might come out in 2026 decided to stay in college for another go-around after it was clear they needed more experience and to refine some parts of their games. That means more prepared passers and less projection in 2027. And I'll go out on a limb and say we get five -- maybe even six -- quarterbacks in Round 1 next April.

We've seen sudden breakout rises to the No. 1 pick in recent years -- like Fernando Mendoza and Joe Burrow -- but it looks like a two-QB race to go first overall right now. First, we have Oregon's Dante Moore, who is only 21 years old, has a ton of support around him and has 20 career starts under his belt. He has phenomenal mechanics and makes every throw look effortless with his arm strength. Moore can place the ball anywhere with his touch and accuracy, too; his 71.8% completion percentage ranked fifth in the FBS last season. If he can play better in the big games, he could be QB1.

Everyone knows about Texas' Arch Manning by now, and he's also a potential No. 1 pick. Like Moore, he has a lot of talent around him, and he comes into 2026 with 15 career starts to his name. He's dangerous with his legs (10 rushing scores last season), and he can make throws rolling out either direction. But I want to see the accuracy jump this year -- you can't be hitting 61.4% of your passes in college and expect to be accurate against tighter pro-level coverage. I'm looking for Manning to complete more of those easy throws and let his athleticism shine.

Beyond Moore and Manning, I feel pretty solid on Ohio State's Julian Sayin, Oklahoma State's Drew Mestemaker and USC's Jayden Maiava going Day 1 ... right now. Sayin is incredibly accurate, and his arm strength is better than advertised. I see some Brock Purdy to his game. Mestemaker is only 20 years old and joins the Cowboys from North Texas, so there is an unknown there -- but I love the traits. And Maiava looked amazing in Week 0, going 25-of-29 for 286 yards and scoring three total touchdowns in a win over San Jose State. He's big and powerful with a live arm.

Then we get into the "maybe" category. Could Notre Dame's CJ Carr build on last season despite losing all of his top offensive skill players to the NFL? Will Ole Miss' Trinidad Chambliss show enough this season for teams to be OK with his smaller 6-foot frame and the fact that he'll be 25 years old before throwing an NFL pass? South Carolina's LaNorris Sellers and UCLA's Nico Iamaleava were each mentioned in last year's predictions file, but they were inconsistent in 2025 and went back to school. Can they take the next step? And I think Miami's Darian Mensah, NC State's CJ Bailey and LSU's Sam Leavitt could all thrive enough to join the conversation, too.

There's probably a dozen guys who could get into Round 1, but that doesn't mean anything unless some of these QBs actually perform. It's probably going to be five first-round quarterbacks when it's all said and done, but I'll leave the door open for someone to rise.

2. Texas, Miami and Georgia will dominate the draft.
Any of these schools could have around 15 players go across the seven rounds. Oregon has really good top-end talent -- receiver Evan Stewart, tight end Jamari Johnson, center Iapani Laloulu, guard Dave Iuli, defensive tackle A'Mauri Washington, edge rusher Matayo Uiagalelei and safety Koi Perich jump to mind -- but the Ducks probably fall slightly behind the Longhorns, Hurricanes and Bulldogs in quantity.

From Miami, I'll highlight cornerback Romanas Frederique Jr. and defensive tackle Ahmad Moten Sr. -- they are both very talented. But I also like Mensah, running back Mark Fletcher Jr., tight end Elija Lofton, edge rusher Damon Wilson II, safety Omar Thornton, defensive lineman Armondo Blount and edge rusher Marquise Lightfoot a lot.

Texas obviously has Manning, but receiver Cam Coleman, offensive tackle Trevor Goosby and edge rusher Colin Simmons could also go very early. Rasheem Biles might be one of the best off-ball linebackers in college football, Jelani McDonald is going to be high on my safety board, and tackle Melvin Siani is going to be key in opening running lanes for both Hollywood Smothers and Raleek Brown.

Georgia doesn't have as many elite prospects. But the list of players with draftable grades is lengthy. Here's a few: cornerback Ellis Robinson IV, running back Nate Frazier, linebackers Raylen Wilson and Chris Cole, safety KJ Bolden and kicker Peyton Woodring.

3. Georgia will have two first-round DBs.
Let's stay with the Bulldogs for a moment. This might not seem wild, but consider that Georgia has never had two defensive backs go in Round 1 of the same draft. It almost happened in 2021, but after Eric Stokes went 29th, Tyson Campbell just missed and went 33rd to open Day 2. But I think we're going to see Robinson and Bolden both go on Day 1 in 2027.

Bolden reminds me a little of Malaki Starks, another safety who patrolled deep for Georgia before going 27th overall in 2025. He makes plays all over the field with his range. The 6-foot, 195-pound junior has three career interceptions over two years, and his 76 tackles ranked second on the team last season. He's a steady player.

Robinson, meanwhile, could easily be in the top 10 or 15 if he plays up to his ability. He had an elite recruiting grade coming out of high school, and after playing just 48 defensive snaps as a freshman, Robinson (6-0, 180) picked off four passes in 2025 as a sophomore. I thought he was more consistent in coverage. I don't think it's completely out of the question for Robinson to push Notre Dame's Leonard Moore for CB1 status.

4. Safety is going to be loaded.
No one is talking about the safeties. It's all about the quarterbacks and some really elite players at cornerback, edge rusher and wide receiver. But I love this safety group, and I think NFL teams are going to have a ton of options at the position. I have roughly 15 safeties graded in Rounds 1-4 right now, including Bolden. The position is both strong at the top and deep.

Notre Dame has two of the biggest names: Brauntae Johnson and Adon Shuler. And they play different styles. Johnson is going to wow everyone at the combine with his athleticism, range and speed. He had four interceptions last season, including a pick-six. He can match and cover on the back end, using his length and burst to make plays.

Shuler, though, is more of a hard-nosed throwback. He's tough and physical, and he hits with power. He had more than 50 tackles for the second straight season in 2025. But don't sleep on his ball skills -- Shuler has five interceptions and 10 pass breakups over the past two years. He's an opportunistic and rugged baller for the Fighting Irish.

5. Jadan Baugh will be RB1.
OK, here's a bolder one. There are a bunch of really good running backs, including Ole Miss' Kewan Lacy. But I'm projecting Baugh to be the first running back off the board -- in the middle part of Round 1. The Florida standout has averaged 5.2 yards per carry over two seasons in Gainesville, and he totaled 1,170 yards and eight touchdowns on the ground last season. But the 6-foot-1, 225-pounder also makes plays out of the backfield as a pass catcher, with 33 receptions for 210 yards and two more scores in 2025.

I just finished watching more tape on Baugh, and I really think he has it all. He moves the chains when he needs to, but he also has the breakaway speed, vision, burst and overall shiftiness to hit home runs. And Baugh is impossible to bring down, with 81 forced missed tackles last season. Lacy, Miami's Fletcher and Missouri's Ahmad Hardy will all get a lot of attention, but Baugh has the talent to come off the board first at the position.

6. Mark Fletcher Jr. will be the highest drafted Miami running back since Willis McGahee.
McGahee went 23rd in 2003. Fletcher likely won't go that high -- I have a second-round grade on him -- but he should get picked earlier than the likes of Frank Gore (No. 65, 2005), Lamar Miller (No. 97, 2012) and Duke Johnson (No. 77, 2015).

Fletcher ran for 1,192 yards and 12 touchdowns last season (with another 140 yards and two scores as a pass catcher), but a lot of that came over four College Football Playoff games. He had 507 yards in the four contests, and he ran for two scores in the title game. His yards per carry jumped from 5.1 during the regular season to 6.8 in the CFP.

I expect Fletcher to pick up where he left off. At 6-foot-2 and 225 pounds, he can dish out punishment on contact. But he's also agile for his size and has the explosion to break off big runs. He went for 10-plus yards 36 times last season, tied for 11th in the country. Fletcher will run you over, but he also has the change-of-direction skills to find open lanes.

7. KJ Duff will be the highest drafted Rutgers skill position player since Kenny Britt.
Britt was 30th overall in 2009. Yes, offensive lineman Anthony Davis (No. 11) and safety Devin McCourty (No. 27) went earlier the following year, but no skill-position player has gone in Round 1 since Britt. The closest were receiver Mohamed Sanu (No. 83, 2012), tight end Tyler Kroft (No. 85, 2015) and Leonte Carroo (No. 86, 2016). But after watching his tape, I think Duff has a legit chance to clip Round 1.

Duff is the definition of matchup nightmare. He's 6-foot-6 and 225 pounds, and any offensive coordinator would love being able to use him as a wideout, "move" tight end or even H-back. He caught 60 balls last season for 1,084 yards (10th in the country), and his 18.1 yards per catch sums up his big-play ability pretty well. Duff uses his size to box out defenders, adjusts well to off-target throws and has the soft hands to complete the catch.

Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith and Texas' Coleman are the pretty clear 1-2 on wide receiver boards right now, but things open up after them. If Duff has a big year, he could fall in the WR3-WR5 range come April.

8. At least three tight ends will get first-round consideration.
Oregon's Johnson is the big name here. He had 510 yards last season at a 15.9 per-catch clip -- despite sharing the tight end spotlight with Kenyon Sadiq, who just went 16th to the Jets in April. At 6-foot-5 and 257 pounds, he has a wide receiver skill set in a tight end's body. Johnson runs well and has a wide catch radius. He's going to be Moore's best friend in that Oregon offense this season.

I see some Kyle Pitts Sr. in LSU's Trey'Dez Green and some T.J. Hockenson in Iowa's DJ Vonnahme. Both join Johnson in carrying a first-round grade. And don't sleep on Texas Tech's Terrance Carter Jr. He was phenomenal last season, displaying some good after-the-catch ability. I have Carter in Round 2 right now, but it wouldn't be shocking to see him join these other three in the Day 1 conversation. This tight end class looks good.

9. Mario Craver is going to rise ... fast.
I can't get enough of Craver's film. People aren't talking about the Texas A&M receiver enough. But he's a star in the making, and I could see him emerging as a first-round candidate. Everyone needs to flip on the Aggies tape and start paying attention to this guy.

I'm not saying he's Zay Flowers, but Craver has similar explosiveness. He's a dynamo with the ball in his hands, and despite being 5-foot-9 and 180 pounds, he displays strength and toughness. Craver plays bigger than his measureables, breaking tackles for extra yards after the catch. Texas A&M featured KC Concepcion last season, but Craver still put up 917 yards (15.5 per reception) and scored five total touchdowns (one rushing). I think we'll see him in the return game more this fall, too, which will only up his draft stock. I love his game -- and come April, I will be joined by a lot of people around the league.

10. Five FCS players will make draft noise.
This is basically my FCS watch list. All five players are probably Day 3 picks, but they all could be contributors at the next level. In no particular order ...

Desmeal Leigh, OT, Youngstown State: Including last Thursday's game against Mercyhurst, Leigh has 39 career starts -- all at left tackle. He's 6-foot-7 and 325 pounds, but I see good movement for his size. He keeps getting better, and my early projection would be the fourth or fifth round.
Marquis Buchanan, WR, Rhode Island: You might recognize this name as an "Orange crusher" from the "First Draft" podcast. Buchanan could become the second Rhode Island draft pick in the past 40 years (Isaiah Coulter, 2020) after leading the FCS in receiving in 2025 with 1,337 yards. At 6-foot-4 and 190 pounds, he can play wherever. His catch radius, YAC traits and deep ball skill set should all get interest from NFL scouts. He got off to a good start to 2026 with 72 yards and a touchdown against Merrimack.
Ty Pennington, QB, Northern Arizona: We haven't heard a Northern Arizona player called on draft weekend since kicker Paul Ernster in 2005, but Pennington has a chance as a late-rounder. He transferred from Pittsburg State in 2024 and has looked great for the Lumberjacks in two seasons. Pennington is accurate and makes good decisions; he refuses to throw interceptions, with just seven over 25 games with the team (including one in Northern Arizona's opener against Eastern Washington on Saturday). And at 6-foot-2 and 220 pounds, he can beat you with his legs, too.
Abu Kamara, S, Yale: He's an instinctive player with five interceptions and 180 tackles over three seasons. Kamara can get into the backfield to create some disruption, too. The 6-foot, 208-pounder had 6.5 tackles for loss and 3.5 sacks last season.
Lance Rucker, Edge, North Dakota: Rucker is a little banged-up, but he's a dang good pass rusher off the edge. His tape shows burst, strength and speed-to-power. At 6-foot-3, 244 pounds, he's explosive with great bend. In 14 games last season, Rucker had 11.5 sacks and 15 tackles for loss. But a foot injury could keep him out for a little while.

Bonus: Championship picks

The Oregon Ducks will win the national championship. I have Moore, Johnson and Co. navigating through the CFP and taking down Notre Dame in the title game. This roster has a lot of really good players who opted to return to school, and Stewart is back off his knee injury to help Moore.

The Cincinnati Bengals will win the Super Bowl. I love my Ravens, but this feels like a big Bengals season to me. Joe Burrow is healthy with two elite receivers at his disposal, and Cincinnati put some resources into the defense this offseason. I see the Bengals beating the Cowboys in Los Angeles next February.

stories.headline: Mike Dean's 'games' claim is 'nonsense' - ex-Premier League ref Graham Scott
stories.summary: Former Premier League referee Graham Scott has accused Mike Dean of "clickbait" following the ex-referee's comments about "playing games" during top-flight matches.
stories.body:
Former Premier League referee Graham Scott has accused Mike Dean of "clickbait" following the ex-referee's comments about "playing games" during top-flight matches.

Dean revealed on Jamie Vardy's podcast this week that, during Premier League matches, he would play secret games that included seeing how long he could go for without giving a foul and his comments have caused considerable controversy.

"There used to be games we used to have, as a laugh we used to say 'Right, we'll kick off now, right. See how long we can go without blowing a whistle,'" Dean said on the podcast.

"I've done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR, obviously. Went 20-25 minutes without blowing a whistle -- 'Let it go, let it go, let it go.'"

Speaking to TalkSport, Scott -- who refereed in the Premier League between 2015 and 2025 -- said that what Dean had revealed about "playing games" was not true.

"I worked with Mike loads of times -- they're not true stories," Scott said. "I wish people wouldn't do this kind of thing. It's the audio equivalent of clickbait, isn't it?

"It's to try and get people interested and laughing. It's palpable nonsense. [...] I found him [Dean] quite shy, personally. I found him quite small when he was in a private situation.

"What happened on the field, what happened in referee meetings is he put on a persona that was way too far the other way, as a kind of coping mechanism."

- Mike Dean admits to playing secret 'game' to not blow whistle while refereeing Premier League matches

- Premier League's summer transfer market is dangerously out of control

- Ranked: Top 50 most expensive Premier League transfers this summer, by true cost

Scott added: "It is dispiriting. I'd challenge Mike, I'd say 'Okay, would you stand in front of the current refs and repeat all those things?' And of course he wouldn't, because they're not true."

Dean's former boss at Professional Game Match Officials Limited (PGMOL), Keith Hackett, insists the referee would not have been able to play the "games" he claims to have done while officiating.

Hackett said on X: "Mike Dean is in fantasy land!! The examination of performances assessors is forensic. When I was boss, referee's performances were forensically examined.

"Dean on my watch could not have done what he said with the monitoring systems in operation."

Hackett added he was "satisfied [Dean] is talking nonsense" and said: "He clearly has damaged his reputation. The fallout does not help current refs."

Pro Ref offered no comment about Dean's claims when approached by ESPN.

Information from the Press Association contributed to this report.

Harwood-Bellis signed for Villa on Tuesday, the Premier League's transfer deadline day, from Championship side Southampton.

He said upon arrival: "The club, in general, being such a prestigious Premier League club. And then you have the added bonus of the Champions League -- it doesn't fill me with anything but excitement.

stories.headline: How the US basketball system has shaped Nigeria's D'Tigress
stories.summary: The United States basketball system has played a major role in the development of Nigeria's national women's basketball team, known as D'Tigress.
stories.body:
The United States basketball system has played a major role in the development of Nigeria's national women's basketball team, known as D'Tigress.

Several players in Nigeria's FIBA Women's World Cup pool were born or developed in the USA, went through the NCAA system, or have connections to the WNBA.

Protland Fire's Amy Okonkwo began her college career at USC before transferring to TCU, where she became the Big 12 Sixth Player of the Year.

Ezinne Kalu played at Savannah State, finishing her career as the first player in program history to score more than 2,000 points.

Elizabeth Balogun's college career took her through Georgia Tech, Louisville and Duke. She was named ACC Freshman of the Year at Georgia Tech and reached the Elite Eight with Louisville before completing her college career at Duke.

Pallas Kunaiyi-Akpanah played four seasons at Northwestern, developing into one of the Big Ten's leading rebounders before spending time with the Chicago Sky.

Promise Amukamara played at Arizona State, while Enabosi starred at Delaware.

Head coach Rena Wakama has connections to both levels herself. She played college basketball at Western Carolina and is now an assistant with the Chicago Sky.

Those ties were evident during Nigeria's World Cup preparation, when D'Tigress played exhibitions against three WNBA teams, the Los Angeles Sparks, Minnesota Lynx and Indiana Fever, before continuing their preparations in China and Europe.

Ezinne Kalu
If there is a heartbeat to this D'Tigress team, it is Kalu. The 34-year-old point guard is the most experienced major-tournament player in Nigeria's current pool, having played at the 2018 World Cup, the Tokyo and Paris Olympics and four Women's AfroBaskets.

Kalu produced arguably the best basketball of her international career in Paris, averaging 18.5 points, four assists and three rebounds in four games.

She remains Nigeria's primary playmaker. At the World Cup qualifying tournament in March, Kalu averaged 9.4 points, 4.8 assists and 2.2 steals per game.

As the team head to Berlin, she is calling for Nigerians in Germany to give D'Tigress something approaching home support.

"We are heading to Berlin for the World Cup, and we need our people there to support us," Kalu said in an Instagram post.

"So we need every Nigerian near Berlin to come through. Bring your flag, your voice and energy."

Amy Okonkwo
Okonkwo has established herself as one of the best players, if not the best, in African basketball. The 6-foot-2 forward has won consecutive Women's AfroBasket MVP awards after leading Nigeria to the 2023 and 2025 championships.

The WNBA player averaged 14 points and six rebounds at the 2025 tournament and scored 19 points while playing all 40 minutes of the final against Mali.

Her ability to score inside, stretch defenses from the perimeter and rebound gives coach Rena Wakama one of her most versatile offensive options.

Berlin will be Okonkwo's World Cup debut, but hardly her first experience at this level. She played at both the Tokyo and Paris Olympics and has been a central figure in Nigeria's last two AfroBasket championships.

At club level, she has traversed Europe, and has also held her own with short but remarkable stints in the WNBA with Dallas Wings, Atlanta Dream and currently Portland.

Victoria Macaulay
The veteran center, who was born in New York, was arguably Nigeria's best performer during the March qualifying tournament. She averaged a team-leading 13.6 points and produced a team-best 16.4 efficiency rating over five games.

The Temple grad brings considerable international experience despite never having played at a World Cup, having represented Nigeria at the Tokyo Olympics and at the 2019 and 2025 AfroBaskets.

Alongside Musa and Pallas Kunaiyi-Akpanah, she gives Nigeria size, experience and physicality in the frontcourt.

Elizabeth Balogun
Balogun could be one of Nigeria's most intriguing players in Berlin. The guard averaged 10.6 points during the qualifying tournament and then produced one of the standout performances of Nigeria's World Cup preparation, scoring 26 points in an 88-77 victory over China in August.

Like Okonkwo, Balogun will be making her World Cup debut despite already having significant global tournament experience. She represented Nigeria at both Tokyo and Paris and was part of the 2023 and 2025 AfroBasket championship teams.

Balogun has also added another American professional connection to the roster after signing a development-player contract with the New York Liberty.

stories.body:
Formula 1 action is back in full swing and next up on the calendar is Monza, also known as the "Temple of Speed."

McLaren's Lando Norris sealed back-to-back victories after winning the Dutch Grand Prix to kick off the second half of the season last time out.

Kimi Antonelli is leading the championship by 59 points and following behind is his teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton both in second.

The Italian youngster will be hit with a grid penalty at his home race for taking a new engine.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know about the Italian Grand Prix.

How to watch

Sky Sports has exclusive F1 rights again in 2026 in the U.K., with every session live on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Italian Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Autodromo Nazionale Monza

The "Temple of Speed" is known for its long straights and heavy braking zones, and is the fastest track in Formula 1 history by overall average lap speed.

It's another classic circuit that has been on the calendar since 1950, only missing one year of racing in 1980 due to upgrading the track infrastructure.

It has one of the best podiums in the world as the famous Ferrari-loving tifosi flood onto the track after the race is finished. It's always a sight to be seen, especially if you are a Ferrari driver or an Italian driver.

Italian Grand Prix

Circuit: Autodromo Nazionale Monza; Monza, Italy

Previous winners
2016: Nico Rosberg, Mercedes

2017: Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes

2018: Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes

2019: Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

2020: Pierre Gasly, AlphaTauri

2021: Daniel Ricciardo, McLaren

2022: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

2023: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

2024: Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

2025: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

Other key stats

First F1 race: 1950

Lap record: 1:18.792, Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Laps: 53 laps of 5.8km. Total distance 306km

Most poles: Lewis Hamilton has seven at this circuit (2009, 2012, 2014-2017, 2020). Other pole sitters from the grid are Fernando Alonso (2007, 2010), Charles Leclerc (2019, 2022), Max Verstappen (2021 and 2025), Carlos Sainz (2023) and Lando Norris (2024).

Most wins: Lewis Hamilton (2012, 2014-2015, 2017-2018) and Michael Schumacher (1996, 1998, 2000, 2003, 2006) are tied on five wins each. Other winners from the current grid are Fernando Alonso (2007, 2010), Pierre Gasly (2020), Charles Leclerc (2019, 2024) and Max Verstappen (2022, 2023 and 2025).

Weather forecast

The weather for the Italian Grand Prix is forecast to be sunny all weekend with light winds, with highs of 32°C on Sunday.

What happened last year?

Max Verstappen set the pace with the fastest lap in F1 history after getting pole position in Monza.

The Dutchman set a time of 1:18.792 breaking Hamilton's record from 2020.

It was McLaren's Norris who was on provisional pole before Verstappen beat him to the line in the closing stages.

Verstappen then went on to win the race in commanding fashion, but there were some team orders taking place at McLaren.

Norris was running in second for the majority of the race, but after a slow pit-stop, the team asked Oscar Piastri to move aside and let him teammate back through for second place.

At the time, Piastri was leading the championship from Norris by 31 points.

Who will win this year?

The biggest news entering the weekend will be Antonelli's engine penalty that will hamper his opportunity to score maximum points during the race.

He leads the championship after winning six races, but title fights can change quickly, as we saw during the backend of the 2025 season.

McLaren's upgrades have certainly been working, but team boss Andrea Stella said that Monza will be the true benchmark in terms of its performance and progress.

Ferrari will be hungry to get a home win with either of its drivers, but Monza will typically suit those strong in straight line speed and high-speed corners, such as Mercedes.

Monza could be one of the best opportunities to close the gap in the title race and take advantage of Antonelli not being a threat at the front of the pack.

stories.headline: What we learned: Pressure can win Hawks the flag; the massive warning sign for Freo
stories.summary: The Hawks' outstanding pressure can win them a premiership, but the Dockers have a big problem after a 'morale-sapping' home qualifying final loss. Here's three things we learned from Hawthorn's win over Fremantle.
stories.body:
Hawthorn produced a stunning performance Thursday evening at Optus Stadium to upset minor premier Fremantle and advance to a second successive preliminary final.

Sam Mitchell's side will now enjoy the week off before returning to the MCG to hunt a place in the 2026 AFL Grand Final. Meanwhile, the Dockers will face the winner of Geelong and Carlton next week in a must-win semifinal.

Here are three things we learned from the game:

Hawthorn's relentless pressure can win the flag
It was a masterclass of pressure and intensity from the Hawks on Thursday evening in the west as they put the Dockers to the sword on their home deck to book their ticket to the final four once again.

The Hawks played the wet-dry conditions perfectly and completely stymied the minor premiers for four quarters. Sam Mitchell's side brought the heat from the opening siren, pressing up and hunting in packs, while never allowing their opponents a moment to breathe and settle into the contest.

They locked the ball inside their attacking forward 50 and had Fremantle's back six under siege for most of the evening, forcing the Dockers into 32 defensive half turnovers -- their most in a game all year. Neither the Docker defense, nor the midfield group, had any answers to stop the onslaught as they again buckled under the finals spotlight.

Mabior Chol set the standard in the opening minutes with two gut-busting efforts inside forward 50. His fleet-footed brigade of small forwards never stood still for a second, while co-captain Jai Newcombe and Dylan Moore were in-and-under all night long, combining for 14 tackles.

It was this insatiable intent and appetite for the contest that allowed Hawthorn to pile on six consecutive goals following Luke Jackson's early opener. The Hawks took a 33-point advantage into the main break, restricting Fremantle to that lone Jackson major. The margin remained the same at the final change and could only be cut to 32 by the final siren.

Thursday's performance was proof the stat sheet can sometimes be a tad misleading. The Dockers dominated total disposals (+74) and enjoyed an advantage in inside 50s (+6), while the clearance and contested possession counts were virtually identical. And yet this game only ever looked like having one victor.

Hawthorn will now enjoy a well-earned week off before returning to the MCG for a preliminary final. The three most likely opponents for that game all reside outside Victoria. If the home crowd support can be paired with the ferocity displayed against Fremantle, there's no reason they can't jag two more wins in 2026.

We should be seriously worried about these Dockers
Fremantle had been the team of the season. Minor premiers with 19 wins and four losses. An even more imposing record at Optus Stadium where they were unbeaten in 12 games, including a sensational come-from-behind win against these Hawks back in Round 9.

Unfortunately for Justin Longmuir and the legion of fans decked head to toe in purple, the Dockers waited until September to turn in their biggest stinker of the year. The Hawks played this game like the final it was and the all-conquering home side never appeared close to being up for the occasion.

Aside from All-Australian running defender Jordan Clark and the reliable Andrew Brayshaw, Fremantle had few winners on the night. Midfielders Shai Bolton and Caleb Serong were well below their best, Murphy Reid left his kicking boots at home, while forward pair Josh Treacy and Jye Amiss were just about unsighted throughout.

Thursday evening was Fremantle's lowest score of the season (40), while the 17 points scored from turnover were the fewest they had managed in a game since 2019 (excluding season 2020 which featured shortened quarters). It was also the club's second-worst game of the year for converting scores from inside 50s.

Fremantle will now have to pick themselves up, dust themselves off, and regroup for a do-or-die semifinal against either Geelong or Carlton next weekend. And while they'll likely be favoured to win that game, would anyone be tipping them with a high degree of confidence?

The loss to the Hawks is as morale-sapping as it gets. Not only because it undoes so much of the great work that was done throughout the year. Not because for them to lift the premiership they'd have to win three straight games, including two on the other side of the country. But because this club, and its supporter base, was adamant it had turned the corner following last year's disappointing home elimination final defeat to Gold Coast.

That one-point loss to end last year's campaign could prove costly 12 months on. All of a sudden the Dockers have lost two finals in a row on their home deck and will be sweating at the prospect of it becoming three in a row next weekend. Meanwhile, what would the Cats or Blues really have to lose?

If you don't want James Sicily at his worst, you don't deserve him at his best
Sure, at times he can play the role of the ultimate villain, but Hawthorn co-captain James Sicily can also be the coolest head you're likely to find behind the ball and one of the greatest assets in football come September.

On Thursday evening he was very much the latter. Sicily was simply sensational against the Dockers, leading the defensive group that completely nullified Fremantle's dangerous three-pronged attack.

Time and time again Sicily out-positioned and out-bodied the Fremantle forwards, drawing on all of his experience and smarts to put on a defensive clinic. He was always in the right place at the right time, always a step ahead of his opponent, and always composed with Sherrin in hand.

Sicily finished his night in the west with a team-high 26 disposals, a game-high 12 intercept possessions, 10 marks, and seven score involvements -- more than any player wearing brown and gold not named Nick Watson.

"We wanted to commit to being tough and taking the game on," Sicily told Fox Sports after the win. "The way we were in sync tonight is just going to give us so much confidence."

There's more than a few Hawks that can make claims to being their club's most important player, but it's hard to look past Sicily when he's in this type of form.

stories.headline: Matías Galarza joins Inter Miami from River Plate
stories.summary: Matías Galarza has joined Inter Miami CF from Argentinian side River Plate.
stories.body:
Matías Galarza officially joined Inter Miami CF from Argentinian side River Plate on Thursday.

The Paraguay midfielder signed a contract with Inter Miami on Wednesday night, officially securing Galarza's move to South Florida on the final day of the MLS transfer window.

Galarza is familiar with MLS have completed a season on loan with Atlanta United FC earlier this year. He recorded one assist in 13 appearances for Atlanta across all competitions -- including MLS regular season games and U.S. Open Cup play.

Galarza also played an integral role for Paraguay at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, scoring one goal in a group stage match against Türkiye and an assist in a shocking round of 32 win over Germany.

Galarza becomes Inter Miami's second signing on deadline day, joining Brazilian winger Riquelme Fillipi, whose deal was confirmed earlier on Wednesday.

The two players join the club as new head coach Cristian Gonzalez takes over for interim manager Guillermo Hoyos.

Inter Miami made several roster moves during this window, with a source confirming to ESPN that defender Noah Allen is set to join the Chicago Fire FC. The two clubs are in advanced negotiations, with a deal set to be finalized shortly.

The MLS secondary transfer window closed at midnight on Wednesday.

Allen was absent from Inter Miami training on Wednesday morning.

Inter Miami also loaned midfielder David Ruiz to the New York Red Bulls, with the Herons receiving $75,000 in 2027 general allocation money for the deal. The Red Bulls also hold the option to make Ruiz's move permanent at the end of the current season.

Inter Miami sits in second place on the Eastern Conference table with 42 points in 22 games.

stories.headline: Winners and losers of Cale Makar's $163.2 million contract
stories.summary: The deal for Colorado's franchise defenseman set a new high benchmark for NHL players, with impacts around the league.
stories.body:
Cale Makar made NHL history last week, becoming the first player to earn $20 million annually in his blockbuster contract extension with the Colorado Avalanche.

His deal is worth $163.2 million over eight seasons. The 27-year-old defenseman's average annual value is $20.8 million against the salary cap. While many anticipated Makar would reset standards with his new contract, the fallout from his deal with Colorado will impact the rest of the NHL.

Some teams, players and trends will end up winners because of it. Others ... not so much.

Here are some winners and losers of the Makar contract.

Winner: Colorado Avalanche
Obviously.

GM Joe Sakic said recently that "you can't win without superstars." That's what you'd expect to hear from a guy who won Stanley Cups as a player on teams that featured Hall of Famers such as Peter Forsberg, Ray Bourque, Rob Blake and this guy Patrick Roy in goal; but also from the guy who built a roster around Makar and center Nathan MacKinnon that produced a Stanley Cup win in 2022.

There's an argument to be made that the Avalanche have the best players in the world at center and on defense and now have them both locked up through 2031. Every team in the league is trying to build a winner. No one has that kind of foundation on which to build.

Sakic was blessed with a star defenseman who wanted to go max term (eight years) from the start of negotiations. No "wait and see" contract. No trying to sync up the end of his deal with that of a family member on another NHL team (more on that in a moment). Cale Makar wanted to give Colorado nine whacks at the piñata while he's under contract.

We can tsk-tsk the Avalanche for not leveraging that commitment into a friendlier cap hit, but the reality is that both Makar and his camp fully understood the current market and the one that Makar could create as an unrestricted free agent next summer. There was no steep discount to be had here, nor should there have been the expectation of one.

There are legit concerns about aging curves and overall health for a player who logs the kind of ice time that Makar does. Teams go into contract talks all the time with that in the back of their throats. But the inherent greatness of Makar, and this window to win with him on the blue line, outweigh those worries.

His cap hit will be recontextualized, as they all eventually are. The NHL is going to have the revenue streams from new media rights deals and at least two new teams inflating the cap during Makar's contract term. As one player agent told me: "By the time this deal is over, there will be guys in the league making $30 million per season."

Loser: Bill Guerin
First off, much respect to the Minnesota GM for facing a barrage of questions during a recent local media tour -- at the Minnesota State Fair, no less! -- about the status of his contract negotiations with Quinn Hughes. We've come to expect that kind of candor from Guerin, as both an NHL executive and U.S. national team general manager, but it's still refreshing when so many of his colleagues get camera shy during high-stakes negotiations.

Guerin told WCCO's Chad Hartman that there's "no tension" with Hughes and his agent, Pat Brisson, but refused to traffic in hypotheticals. Dan Barreiro of KFAN told Guerin he "can't trade" Hughes due to how much the Wild gave the Vancouver Canucks for the defenseman; Guerin reiterated that "we don't want to lose him and our fans don't want to lose him."

Hughes has one more season left at $7.85 million before becoming an unrestricted free agent next summer, and he's eligible to sign an extension now. If he signs before Sept. 15, he can max out at an eight-year term. If he signs as a free agent next summer, the max is six years -- although the max contract he could sign (20% of a projected $113.5 million cap in 2027-28) would be higher, at $22.7 million.

It's hard to find many around the NHL who believe Hughes will sign a long-term deal with the Wild. Most expect it'll be a three-year term that walks him up to 2030 when his brother Jack Hughes of the New Jersey Devils is an unrestricted free agent. But what about the money?

As Guerin did radio hits about Hughes amid the butter sculptures and lumberjack shows at the fair, there was one common theme: That Makar's deal impacts what Hughes could make on a new contract, but not dramatically.

"Could it affect you financially? Yeah. There's the bar with Cale Makar signing that contract in Colorado, but Quinn might be after different things. He's got different things in the life that's important to him," he told Hartman.

Guerin's theory: That Hughes has already made significant money in his career, so he can afford to make different types of decisions on his next contract. His current contract, signed in 2021, is worth $47.1 million.

"It doesn't have to be that 'Makar signed for this so he's got to sign for that.' No. He can do whatever the hell he wants because he's not going broke tomorrow," Guerin told KFAN.

Of course, Makar will have made $54 million on his current deal before starting on a $163 million contract in 2027-28.

It's possible that Guerin would have to overcompensate Hughes regardless of what Makar makes, like he did to keep Kirill Kaprizov in Minnesota. Makar's deal doesn't dramatically change the math on Hughes. It also doesn't uncomplicate what's already an extremely complicated negotiation for Guerin.

Winner: Matthew Schaefer
After just one season with the New York Islanders -- in which he was the unanimous choice for NHL rookie of the year -- Schaefer might already be in blank check territory for his next contract. The defenseman, who turns 19 this week, has that rare franchise-altering alchemy of on-ice ability and off-ice charisma that's been previously exhibited by players like Alex Ovechkin. He's that special.

And soon he'll be very, very rich.

Schaefer can sign an extension next summer as he enters the last year of his rookie contract. Islanders GM Mathieu Darche now has two contractual magnets pulling up Schaefer's salary: Makar, resetting the bar for defensemen at $20.4 million AAV; and San Jose Sharks phenom Macklin Celebrini, another transformative young player who will earn $18.8 million annually over five seasons.

Loser: Columbus Blue Jackets
The current holy trinity of NHL defensemen is Makar, Hughes and Zach Werenski, the latter of whom won the Norris Trophy last season ... and then blocked a trade to the Dallas Stars after communicating that he didn't plan on signing an extension with the Blue Jackets.

Werenski, 29, has since emphasized that he wants to remain in Columbus as long as the Blue Jackets are a playoff team that's trending in the right direction.

He's eligible to sign an extension next summer, with two years remaining on a deal that carries a $9,583,334 average annual value. The ceiling for Werenski as a 2028 free agent would be an AAV of $24.6 million. Whether or not his heart's still in Columbus could be a separate issue from whether the Blue Jackets would commit that kind of money for any player -- let alone a defenseman who will be in his early 30s by then.

Winner: Montreal Canadiens
Lane Hutson finished one point behind Cale Makar in scoring among defensemen last season. In 2027-28, when he's 23 years old, Hutson will count $11.55 million less against the salary cap than Makar does.

There are mitigating circumstances for Montreal's deal with Hutson, which he signed last October in the final season of his rookie contract. The defenseman was a 10.2(c) restricted free agent, leaving him with little leverage as a player ineligible for either an offer sheet or arbitration. But Montreal used that advantage to squeeze an eight-year deal with an $8.85 million annual cap hit out of Hutson.

It was praised as a bargain at the time -- many felt he'd at least hit $10 million AAV -- but given how the ground shifted after Makar's deal for scoring defensemen, it's an absolute steal.

This is going to be for Montreal like MacKinnon's second contract was for Colorado (seven years at $6.3 million annually): an epic underpayment of an elite player that allows his team to get a ton of other business done. Keep in mind the Avalanche won the Stanley Cup in Year 6 of that deal.

Loser: Analytics truthers
Cale Makar has been a Norris Trophy finalist in six of his seven NHL seasons, winning it twice and finishing second in the voting twice as well. He has a Calder Trophy and a Conn Smythe to his credit. He's considered the best defenseman of his generation, perhaps even the best player of his generation. Comparisons to Bobby Orr aren't met with a scoff but with respectful contemplation.

But there's another assessment of Makar -- in the present and for the duration of his contract -- that's worth considering: The one from analytics-driven skeptics who see Makar's deified status as more than a little bit owed to the greatness of MacKinnon.

Corey Sznajder had a nuanced look at this theory on All Three Zones, which included these numbers from Natural Stat Trick:

"Over the past three seasons, Makar has shared the ice with MacKinnon for 2,572 minutes compared to 1,434 minutes without him (all 5v5 by the way). In those minutes, the Avs own 58.1% of the shot attempts, 57.4% of the expected goals and 61.3% of the goals. In the minutes with Makar without MacKinnon the ice, Colorado owns only 47.3% of the shots, 48% of the expected goals and 52.2% of the goals. MacKinnon without Makar on the ice is at 56.6%, 55.7% and 66.8% in all three of those stats respectively," Sznajder wrote.

Those kinds of stats don't necessarily paint their on-ice partnership as symbiotic, but rather MacKinnon being the one driving the bus, while Makar stands over his shoulder like Keanu with Sandra Bullock in "Speed."

Obviously, the Avalanche don't care about any of this after giving Makar a record-breaking contract. He and MacKinnon are going to share the ice for Colorado until 2031 at a minimum. But this conjecture will continue to simmer in awards debates, player comparisons on social media and now in evaluating Makar under this megadeal.

Winner: player empowerment
As I wrote in June, the age of player empowerment is at hand for the NHL. We saw it in Brady Tkachuk leveraging a trade to his brother's team in South Florida, or in Dylan Larkin trying to force his way out of a long-term commitment to the Detroit Red Wings. But we also saw it in some of the mega-contracts that we signed in the offseason, with Makar's deal as the current apex.

Young stars like Celebrini ($18.8 million AAV) and Chicago's Connor Bedard ($15 million AAV) scored big in re-signing with their teams. Leo Carlsson shocked the NHL by signing a five-year, $18 million AAV offer sheet with the Philadelphia Flyers that the Anaheim Ducks matched.

(My favorite theory of the offseason, offered up by one NHL player agent: That Flyers ownership greenlit the Carlsson offer sheet as the ultimate long-term vengeance in the Cutter Gauthier drama with Anaheim. "They probably want to say, 'Hey, Philly's a good spot to be in. Don't [mess] with us.'")

There are always going to be players who take a "team-friendly" deal because the circumstances warrant it, like Connor McDavid earning less annually than Leon Draisaitl. But the ones breaking the bank are no longer the outliers, and they're going to keep breaking it. Some NHL teams are projecting the salary cap could rise to $150-$160 million by the 2031-32 season. Makar is just the beginning.

(Although, technically, Makar did just sign a team-friendly deal: $400,000 annually under the max, and one year before unrestricted free agency could have upped his ask to over $22 million annually.)

Loser: Short-term deals
Perhaps the most shocking aspect of Makar's extension wasn't the money but the term.

One hallmark of the NHL's player empowerment trend has been contract duration. Auston Matthews was one of the first huge names to go short-term, signing a five-year deal with the Toronto Maple Leafs in 2019 and then a four-year extension in 2023. Since then, Celebrini, Bedard, Carlsson and Nico Hischier of the New Jersey Devils have all signed five-year extensions, while defenseman Evan Bouchard went four years with the Edmonton Oilers.

But Makar's focus from the start of talks with the Avalanche was an eight-year term, an option that will not exist when the new CBA kicks in later this month.

"I think it gives us a lot of clarity in the sense of the direction we want to go in, hopefully being able to succeed in the next nine years, and have that stability in knowing that the contract is there and we have the pieces that we can build around," he said, via NHL.com.

Again, not everyone in the NHL can look around their locker room and see Nathan MacKinnon, with the proof of concept of having already won a Stanley Cup with him. Makar didn't have to take the "wait and see" deal that others in his tax bracket have with teams striving to become contenders. Makar knows what he has around him. And now, the Avalanche know they have Makar for the next decade.
