stories.headline: NRL: Benji Marshall eyeing Tyson Frizell as Tigers seek to bolster pack
stories.summary: Wests Tigers have emerged as a potential landing spot for veteran Newcastle forward Tyson Frizell, with the club interested in bringing the former NSW and Australia representative to Concord next season.
stories.body:
Wests Tigers have emerged as a potential landing spot for veteran Newcastle forward Tyson Frizell, with the club interested in bringing the former NSW and Australia representative to Concord next season.

ESPN understands the Tigers have identified Frizell as a recruitment target as they continue to shape their roster for 2027.

Frizell, 34, is off contract at the end of the season and remains without a deal for next year as Newcastle turns its attention towards its finals campaign.

The experienced back-rower would add another hardened presence to a Tigers forward pack that has increasingly been built around a younger core.

Fonua Pole and Samuela Fainu have established themselves as key members of Benji Marshall's pack, while former Newcastle forward Kai Pearce-Paul joined the club this season and has added another long-term option on an edge.

Frizell would bring more than 300 games of NRL experience across Cronulla, St George Illawarra and Newcastle, along with an extensive representative resume for NSW and Australia.

Despite being in the latter stages of his career, Frizell has remained a reliable presence for Newcastle this season and continues to play significant minutes on an edge.

That experience would provide another senior presence for a Tigers roster preparing to undergo further change in 2027.

Jarome Luai will depart Concord at the end of the season to join Parramatta, leaving the Tigers without one of the most experienced members of their spine and leadership group.

The club has also fallen short of a long-awaited return to finals football this season, extending a drought that dates back to 2011.

The Tigers have already begun adding experience to their roster for next year, with Jayden Brailey set to arrive from Canberra, as exclusively reported by ESPN in July, while the club continues to survey the market in a bid to strengthen Marshall's squad.

Frizell has spent the past six seasons in Newcastle after joining the Knights from the Dragons ahead of the 2021 season.

For now, the veteran's immediate focus remains on Newcastle's finals campaign as the Knights prepare for their first game of the postseason.

stories.headline: Orlando Magic offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: Can a change in leadership unlock Orlando's big three? Offseason recap and early looks at the 2026-27 season.
stories.body:
The Orlando Magic appear to be trending in the right direction and are looking to bounce back from an injury-riddled season and build on the momentum of their short-lived but memorable run in last season's playoffs.

Two of the Magic's stars, Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner, missed significant time last season, hindering Orlando's consistency on offense. However, after parting with head coach Jamahl Mosley in May, the Magic brought on Sean Sweeney to hopefully build on the team's elite defense and unlock their scoring.

However, in an increasingly competitive Eastern Conference, reaching contention will be harder now more than ever for a team still searching for its stride. What will the season look like with a finally healthy Magic team and new leadership?

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more.

Quick links:

Roster | Depth chart | Transactions

More Magic coverage | More NBA

Offseason at a glance
Key additions: C Nikola Vucevic, G Izaiyah Nelson

Key subtractions: F Moritz Wagner, G Jett Howard

Key retentions: F Jonathan Isaac, G Jevon Carter

The Magic's biggest move this offseason was hiring Sean Sweeney to replace Jamahl Mosley. Orlando also brought Nikola Vucevic back on a one-year, $3.9 million deal since trading him in 2021 and will use his ability to score and shoot to space the floor for Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner and Desmond Bane. The Magic blew a 3-1 lead over top-seeded Detroit in the first round of the playoffs after Wagner went down due to injury and were in desperate need of someone who can get easier baskets and make outside shots. Vucevic should help. Moe Wagner departed for Brooklyn via free agency, separating Franz from his brother for the first time in his pro career. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Zach Kram's offseason grade: D+

Former franchise center Vucevic is returning on a minimum contract, but the Magic have otherwise sat out the offseason since hiring Sean Sweeney as their new coach. Once again, it seems, they're hoping for better health and internal development to fix their problems and vault them out of the middle of the Eastern Conference standings next season. -- Kram

What we learned this offseason
From Ben Golliver's offseason lessons piece: The Magic just wanted a new voice.

Orlando came awfully close to winning its first playoff series since 2010 last season, but instead it blew a 3-1 lead against the Detroit Pistons and suffered its third consecutive first-round exit. That demoralizing ending, which followed months of reported tension between Jamahl Mosley and his players, led to the coach's dismissal.

The Magic hired well-regarded San Antonio Spurs assistant Sean Sweeney to replace Mosley, then decided to keep the bulk of its playoff rotation intact. In fact, Orlando's five highest-paid players -- Banchero, Wagner, Bane, Jalen Suggs and Wendell Carter Jr. -- will all return. That group deserves another shot, as it logged just 182 minutes together last season due to a string of injuries.

Sweeney has extensive experience working with stars during his previous stops with the Milwaukee Bucks and Dallas Mavericks, so hopefully he will be able to coax more efficient scoring from Banchero. But the Magic's path to postseason progress begins with their defense: Orlando slipped from second in defensive efficiency in 2024-25 to 13th last season. A reversal of that trend under Sweeney could have the Magic competing for a top-four playoff seed next season. -- Golliver

The big question: Can Sweeney unlock the Magic big three?
Orlando's front office believes the Magic can be the team it envisioned, contending in the East with a stingy defense and a young core. They saw the potential when Orlando looked destined to turn around a disappointing season by getting out of the Play-In last season and coming close to eliminating the East's top team in Detroit.

Can Sweeney find a way to get the best out of Banchero, Wagner and Bane? Regarded as one of the top defensive-minded head coaches in waiting and a grinder known for helping develop stars like Giannis Antetokounmpo in Milwaukee, Sweeney will have to get Banchero and Wagner on the same page, keeping them healthy and finding a way to improve the Magic's offense and outside shooting. He also is expected to turn an already stellar defense into an elite one. -- Youngmisuk

Basketball Power Index rank: No. 16
Here are the predicted Net Points per 100 possessions for the Magic's top seven players for the 2026-27 season:

Banchero has shot an effective 53% from the field in his career. That is lower than all top five picks in every draft since 2018, except for last year's Rookie of the Year, Cooper Flagg, by the tiniest amount.

Orlando has five players in its rotation who were taken in the top eight of the draft. Wagner and Carter are the two that are ahead of the average performance at their pick number. -- Dean Oliver

Read about how Net Points works here.

Biggest X factor this season
G Jalen Suggs

The Magic become a much more talented team when Suggs is available and playing at his best, but two key questions surround the combo guard in his age-25 season. First, can he stay on the court? Suggs' 57 games last season were the second-most in his career, and he's exceeded 1,600 minutes just once. Second, can Suggs shoot? He made 40% of his 3s in 2023-24 but has regressed to 31% and 34% over the last two seasons. -- Kram

Betting insight from our expert
Bet to make ahead of the season: The Magic will participate in the play-in tournament (+110)

The Magic have participated in the play-in tournament in each of the past two seasons, winning 45 games last season and 41 the season before. They battled injuries to key players during both seasons, particularly to young stars Banchero and Wagner, so with complete health they have the upside to improve. On the other hand, the Eastern Conference has become tougher this offseason, so it will likely be more difficult to earn a top-6 seed this season than in recent seasons. All told, the Magic project to be a team in the bottom half of the top-10 in the East, giving them a good chance to be in the play-in for the third straight season. -- Andre Snellings

stories.headline: Inside the world of high-stakes NFL survivor pools: Las Vegas, 'Meatball Brothers' -- and a $20 million prize
stories.summary: In the heart of Las Vegas, bettors try to do the unthinkable: turn $1,000 into $20 million throughout the NFL season.
stories.body:
LAS VEGAS -- JOSHUA NORTHCUTT STEPS inside the sports betting temple that is the Circa Resort & Casino in the heart of downtown. He walks past the iconic neon figure of Vegas Vickie and into Circa's famed sportsbook, a monument to the sports betting experience with its stadium-style chairs and a three-story tall screen showing the sports action of the day.

Northcutt holds $1,000 cash in his hand. The 36-year-old aircraft parts lead traveled from Cincinnati to the 2026 Ultimate Contest Weekend to throw his hat in the ring for potential life-changing money -- over $20 million. He's processed his bankroll for the season and has already subtracted the $1,000 entry fee for Circa Survivor, hoping it is a worthy investment of his "fun money." Still, having just bought a house with his girlfriend and child, there are some nerves as he approaches the betting window.

The competition attracts clientele from all walks of life. Professional poker players mingle with retired golf buddies pooling money together; a first-time player like Northcutt can share the spotlight with celebrities such as Baseball Hall of Fame pitcher Greg Maddux and UFC president Dana White, who both entered the contest in 2025.

"Just the challenge of it specifically with this contest, I guess competing against a lot of the experts just to see where I compare on a level to them," Northcutt told ESPN of why he wanted to enter. "Should I really even be doing this? Is this a waste of money?"

A longtime staple of pools run by friends, family or coworkers, the survivor contest format is one of the most enduring forms of football betting. But here, Circa Survivor has positioned itself at the forefront of the NFL betting contests.

The premise is simple enough: Pick one NFL team to win outright each week (including two holiday mini-weeks) with the caveat that one team cannot be picked twice. Lose, and you're out. Survive to a perfect 20-0 record and you claim a share -- or all of -- at least a $20 million top prize.

"The idea of turning $1,000 into a share of millions is obviously everyone's dream in gambling," Jason Somerville, a poker pro who won the contest in 2025 as part of a team, told ESPN.

"It's sort of like the World Series of Poker main event in terms of you're trying to win the big one. There's certainly a lot of that sort of aspirational element that's nice and in sports betting, you don't really have that that often."

Pro football survivor contests are experiencing a boom akin to poker in the mid-2000's, in some respects due to the existence of Circa's flagship competition as well as the ease of access to online organization platforms, which are beginning to leak into the high-stakes world themselves. As of the second day of Circa's Ultimate Contest Weekend -- when the company invites potential contestants to sign up -- there were over 14,000 entries.

As the big games have grown and word-of-mouth has spread, more football fans are being exposed to the "incredibly elegant, beautiful design," as Galen Hall, a pro poker player and 2025 Circa Survivor winner, puts it.

"The survivor format, it's so simple that anyone can get into it. It doesn't take knowing a bunch of extra stuff except who you want to win and who you want to lose," said Gabe Patgorski, another Circa Survivor champion and founder of research website Survivor Atlas. "There's something where it's like in our nature as humans, there's some natural instinct of just surviving where the format is tapping into something more natural than any other gaming format there is.

"It's so much simpler and it resonates with something deep in us more so than fantasy sports or poker or sports betting ever could."

CIRCA'S LEADERSHIP AIMS to find ways to adapt to the competition (such as the introduction of the holiday mini weeks) yet keep it true to this simplistic nature, according to Circa Sports director of operations Jeff Benson.

"We wanted to figure out how to make the contest harder but not take away the core tenets of what made survivor, survivor," Benson told ESPN. "We've gotten pretty lucky from a scheduling perspective that things have really worked out that over the years we've been able to build from 17 games to 20."

The first contest in 2020 attracted 1,390 entries with 35 going the distance; the 2025 edition brought in 18,718 entries with only five making it the whole way. The changes had the desired effect, with veteran players calling the holiday slates easily the most stressful time of the season. Since the schedule expanded, players have adopted intricate strategies.

"As a casual football fan, you can start picking, look at it every week and spend 10 minutes on it, and it's enjoyable and fun. Or you can do like tens of thousands of hours of analysis and really get some reward from that," Hall said. "To pick up and start playing, there's no barrier. But the amount of complexity that's actually involved in playing it well is incredible."

Hall believes there are different levels to thinking about survivor picks, ranging from picking a team for football reasons alone, to modeling out future picks, to understanding the expected value (EV) of your entries with the possibility of buying, selling or splitting equity on them. Additionally, Hall fully recognizes the luck factor as well.

"It's a good balance," he said. "If it's too much skill, the casual players get chopped up too quickly and don't come back. And then if it's too much luck, you might as well play the lotto."

Knowing the value of one's entry and treating it like a commodity is essential for many high-level players: The longer the contest goes on, and the more players are eliminated, the more each entry's value theoretically increases above the initial $1,000.

There are third-party marketplaces that will facilitate the purchase or sale of partial or full entries, and near the end of the season, players will sometimes negotiate amongst each other to chop the pot to ensure they each get a share of the grand prize. Players will also often hedge their picks, with Circa even offering lines of credit for big bets to guarantee players don't go home empty-handed.

Players realize that they increase their potential equity in the top prize by having more entries -- and that they can gain more entries by teaming up.

The Circa Survivor rules allow each individual player to have up to 10 entries in their name, but there is no rule saying they can't take those 10 entries and combine them into a group with however many other players. From there, with all the money pooled, players can either collaborate on a strategy -- as was the case with Somerville and Patgorski -- or allow one player to make the picks for everyone, as Hall did to get two entries across the finish line last season.

"Even though those people have a better chance of winning, they're paying such a big multiplier for it that a lot of their picks end up being minus EV because they're trying to cover multiple different scenarios," poker pro and Circa contestant David Baker told ESPN. "So you're getting more leverage on some of them. Some of them try to spread it out so much that it's basically impossible for them to get too many of them to advance."

And just because it's less likely for a single entry to win doesn't mean it's impossible.

"They still can't stop an individual from going 20-0," Patgorski said. "That's kind of the great equalizer."

Many of the syndicates are made up of groups of friends who treat it as a communal betting experience. In 2024, a group of six coworkers at a meat processing company pooled together their financial resources to buy three entries and appropriately named their team "The Meatball Brothers."

After a notoriously nightmarish first three weeks that saw the most popular pick lose each week and only 4.5% of the original entries remain, the Brothers were down to one entry. But that one made it all the way to Week 18, when the team came to Vegas to watch their pick win. Each member was guaranteed over $300,000 in contest prize money, plus additional winnings from a spread hedge against the pick.

"We're a bunch of average dudes and we won this whole goddamn thing," said Carson Williams, one of the Meatball Brothers.

WHEN VISITORS COME to the area of southern Nevada collectively known as Las Vegas, they usually hop off the plane at Harry Reid International Airport and make their way to the famed Strip, technically located in the unincorporated towns of Paradise and Winchester. The Strip has created much of the public perception and lore surrounding Vegas, but about six miles away from the glitz and glamor, Derek Stevens built his casino empire on Fremont Street, the historic center of Downtown Las Vegas.

It's here that Circa broke ground and instantly became one of the most popular resorts in the area.

After years of buying up old casino resorts in the area and refurbishing them, Stevens opened Circa in 2020. His goal from the beginning was to make it a central hub for sports bettors and knew he could quickly build that reputation by running a traditional NFL handicapping contest in the mold of the Westgate's famed SuperContest, so the casino launched Circa Million in 2019. A year later, it started Survivor.

"We hit lightning in a bottle, [and] Circa Survivor just absolutely took off," Stevens said. "I did it just with my buddies 35 years ago and I thought, 'Oh my God, what a game.' So I've been playing for a long time and there's nothing like the energy or adrenaline you get. Even when you make a bet, there's nothing like a survivor pick."

To further push the envelope, Circa launched Grandissimo in 2025, a $100,000 per entry version of Survivor that garnered 69 entries in its first season.

All of Circa's contests are "no rake," meaning that all of the money from entry fees goes directly into the pot and the house does not take a cut. In that sense, Circa does not profit directly from the contest and even spends considerable money marketing it and putting it on, according to Stevens and Benson.

But Circa does make plenty of money back in ancillary purchases at its property and builds valuable brand power, mostly thanks to Nevada state laws. The Nevada Gaming Control Board (NGCB) dictates that any organization running a sports pool in the state must have its patrons register for the contest and place their weekly picks in person, meaning that every participant in the tournament must make the pilgrimage to Downtown Las Vegas before football season if they want to participate.

"We said, 'OK, let's create some great experiences throughout the summer for people to come to Las Vegas,'" Stevens said. "It's a massive deal when you think about how many people enter the contest, and that means in the slowest time of the year in Vegas, shoot, we're going to have 35,000 entries [between the three contests] in July, August and early September."

It's especially relevant amid the city's pronounced tourism slump, which saw the city host 3.1 million fewer visitors in 2025 than the year before, according to data from the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority.

Circa and Nevada's insistence on keeping pro football contests in-state also gave rise to proxy services. While it is illegal for someone to make a bet on someone's behalf, the NGCB has made an exception for the contests, allowing proxies to make picks for contestants each week, so long as the player signed up on their own first.

Between 85% and 90% of Circa Survivor participants use a proxy service, according to Circa. Matty Simo and Toni Law -- who co-own FootballContest.com, one of the players in the proxy industry -- recognize the value the in-person aspect brings not only to their business but to Circa's.

"If you go back 30-some years or whatever, to when the SuperContest and some of the other casinos in Las Vegas started doing football contests, the main purpose, especially since there's no rake involved, is that they want to bring people into the property," Simo said. "I don't think anybody would really know much about Circa if it wasn't for the contests and the ability to see the property, see what it's all about. ... It's just a huge marketing opportunity for them."

FOR ALL OF the prestige and spectacle the in-person Las Vegas football contest experience provides, there's an argument to be had that it's simply old-fashioned and behind the times in a digital world.

In June, peer-to-peer gaming platform Splash Sports and prediction market Polymarket announced a new partnership that would see them host a $1,000 per entry pro football survivor contest that will notably guarantee $21 million in prize money.

The contest will allow up to 150 entries per user and will feature six "double pick" weeks where players must select two teams instead of one, an apparent foil to Circa's holiday mini weeks. It will also feature a built-in marketplace for buying and selling partial or full entries and is available to play online across much of Canada and 35 U.S. states (but, of course, not in Nevada).

TJ Ross, Splash's co-founder and co-CEO, says he has been a fan of survivor since he was a kid, citing the format's "minimum amount of effort for the maximum amount of sweat." When he saw the opportunity to partner with Polymarket -- with its bountiful financial heft -- to bring a challenger to the market, he knew he had to take it.

"I think the contests in Vegas created structure around it and what we're really trying to do is democratize it so anyone can play from anywhere," Ross said.

The Splash survivor contest is a natural competitor to Circa's product, but many of the latter's veteran players don't necessarily see it that way. Hall, Patgorski and Somerville all say they'll probably throw at least an entry or two into the Splash contest in addition to their usual helping of Circa entries, though not every potential player will have that luxury.

These veterans ultimately believe the top players will always keep coming back to the original big contest. Patgorski recalls that Chris Moneymaker's win at the 2003 World Series of Poker main event sparked an explosion in the poker industry, with online platforms all offering massive payouts to try and ride the wave.

"The main event in Las Vegas has always been the best poker tournament in the world," Patgorski said. "My gut says it's kind of going to be like that in survivor, where Circa is always going to be the best one to play."

If there's one thing on which Circa can continue to pride itself on, it's the community it created when it compels its players to convene during the oppressively hot Nevada summer. In the more tolerable winter, some of them come back for a celebration of victory and the fitting of their blue winner's jackets. Or on the other hand, a dirge of defeat, as one player, Pete Tarsiewicz, experienced two years in a row when his entry lost in Week 18 of the 2024 and 2025 seasons.

"It's just something we have circled on our calendar every year," said Aman Dhaddey, a software engineer from Vancouver, who plays Million. "It's one of those things: birthdays, Christmas, Circa entry."

This year's Ultimate Contest Weekend felt like a convention or reunion, where long-lost friends met to catch up, gamble and talk about the upcoming season. The Meatball Brothers, who strengthened their bond with each other through the game, call the community which plays the contests a family.

Northcutt is thrilled to join, which he had at first only experienced from afar through listening to the "Sports Gambling Podcast." Here in Downtown Las Vegas, he's rubbing shoulders with those media personalities and pro bettors, finalizing his Week 1 pick -- possibly the Los Angeles Chargers over the lowly Arizona Cardinals, as many contestants are also eyeing -- and planning out a path to glory.

"I am competing against experts, but it's also average fans like me coming out and enjoying it and just carrying on conversations, meeting new people," he said. "It's a little bit outside my box to do this, but I enjoy it. It's hard not to get a feel of the excitement that everybody's having because we all got the same chance."

stories.headline: Impact of 12 MLB stars' down 2026 seasons on their teams
stories.summary: From bad gameplay to injuries to a mix of both, these players' seasons had huge impact on the success of their clubs this year.
stories.body:
Last October, Cal Raleigh and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. faced off against each other in the ALCS. Raleigh was coming off a 60-homer campaign, and Guerrero went off over the course of the postseason, hitting .397 with eight home runs and 15 RBIs in 18 games.

Their encore performances in 2026, however, have been a disaster. Raleigh, while hot of late (he was the AL Player of the Week last week), is still hitting just .172 with 20 home runs, with fewer hits (64) than the 65 home runs he totaled in 2025. Guerrero has a .693 OPS and remarkably hasn't homered in Toronto all season.

Those two aren't the only stars of 2025 who have suffered through injuries or performance issues this season. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge hasn't played since May 31 due to a stress fracture in his right rib. Garrett Crochet, last year's AL Cy Young runner-up, has missed most of the season. Juan Soto, Francisco Lindor and Hunter Brown missed time with injuries. Jose Ramirez has had his worst season since he was a part-time player in 2015. Julio Rodriguez is on track for the lowest batting average, on-base percentage and slugging percentage in his five seasons in the majors. Paul Skenes is trying to keep his ERA under 4.00 instead of 2.00. Trea Turner finished fifth in the NL MVP voting a year ago with 5.4 WAR but has been below replacement level in 2026.

Indeed, this has been one of the most important storylines of the season: the fallen stars of 2026. We'll look at how some of these performances have affected the playoff races, but first let's check: Is 2026 an outlier?

You would expect any group of players who had great seasons to be collectively less valuable the following season. To check out how 2026 compared to other seasons, I went back to 1995 and used Baseball-Reference WAR to see how the top 10 players in the MVP voting and top three in the Cy Young voting fared the following season. This gave a list of 21 to 26 players for each year, depending on how many pitchers finished in the top 10 of MVP voting (for National League pitchers in the pre-DH era, only pitching WAR was considered). WAR numbers for 1995 were prorated to 162 games, as were the current figures for 2026.

It turns out that, yes, 2026 has seen a pretty extreme decline in value -- and these numbers don't even include Guerrero, who finished 13th in the MVP voting so wasn't included in the study. The 2025 group of 23 players combined for 145.1 WAR and are on pace for 87.2 WAR in 2026, a 39.9% decrease. That would be the third-largest decline since 1995:

1. 2011-12: 44.0%

2. 2009-10: 42.8%

3. 2025-26: 39.9%

4. 1995-96: 39.5%

5. 2004-05: 38.0%

The average year-to-year decline in value is 31.3%, with a low of 16.6% from the 2017 group. While a high starting value of collective WAR can affect the following season's decline, that wasn't the case for our 2025 group of top 10 MVP/top three Cy Young finishers. The average WAR of 6.3 per player is right at the overall average of 6.3 over the 29 years in the study.

Obviously, these declines have had a big impact on the success of these players' teams this season. Let's dive into the causes behind their down years, as well as the extent of that impact.

Cal Raleigh, Seattle Mariners (7.2 WAR to 0.9)

Primary cause: Higher strikeout rate; much lower hard-hit rate; can't catch up to fastballs; might have played through an oblique strain earlier in the season before finally going on the injured list for a month.

The Mariners finished ninth in the majors in runs per game in 2025 with Raleigh leading the way. This year? They're last, at 3.96. That's not all on Raleigh, but after creating an estimated 49 runs above average in 2025, he's at seven runs below average in 2026, a 56-run difference. The Mariners are on pace to score 124 fewer runs than last season.

Julio Rodriguez, Seattle Mariners (6.6 WAR to 2.5)

Primary cause: Declining hard-hit rate (95th percentile as a rookie, career-low 65th percentile in 2026); unimproved chase rate; poor defensive metrics.

Like we said, it's not all on Raleigh. J-Rod was 24 runs above average in 2025 and is just two runs above average in 2026 -- with a significant decline in his defensive metrics as well (plus-9 runs saved in 2025, minus-4 in 2026).

Rodriguez was so good as a 21-year-old rookie in 2022 that his future seemed unlimited, a player who would contend for MVP awards on an annual basis. But his batting average and on-base percentage have declined each season as he hasn't made the adjustments that we've seen other players make, such as Pete Crow-Armstrong this season. At times, J-Rod has been one of the top all-around players in the league -- the Mariners can only hope that 2026 won't be a permanent step backward.

Vladimir Guerrero Jr. (4.6 to 0.9), Toronto Blue Jays

Primary cause: Shocking lack of power; declining chase rate (89th percentile in 2025 to 44th percentile); drop in number of "barrels."

George Springer (4.8 to 0.8), Toronto Blue Jays

Primary cause: Struggled against fastballs; more ground balls; lower rate of "fast swings" leading to a lower hard-hit rate (78th percentile down to 36th percentile).

Guerrero didn't finish in the top 10 of the MVP voting, but Springer did -- and his OPS has dropped from .959 last season to .743. Springer's decline was certainly more predictable, given that his 2025 season was the highest adjusted OPS of his career (at age 35). With Guerrero and Springer leading the decline, the Blue Jays have dropped from 4.93 runs per game, fourth in the majors in 2025, to 29th in 2026 at around 4.00, better than only ... the Mariners.

Paul Skenes, Pittsburgh Pirates (8.0 WAR to 2.4)

Primary cause: Worse luck on balls in play; four-seamer velo has dropped from 98.2 mph to 96.9 (although it appears to be a deliberate choice in an attempt to stay healthy); changeup has been less effective; .309 average allowed with runners in scoring position compared to .181 in 2025.

This is a shocking one given Skenes' 1.96 ERA through his first two seasons in the majors and because it doesn't appear to be injury-related (that we know), like most of the year-to-year declines you'll see from pitchers. The Pirates are 5 games out of the final wild card, so a better Skenes would have them right there in the playoff picture. While he has certainly seen some bad BABIP (batting average on balls in play) luck with a porous Pittsburgh defense behind him, that alone doesn't explain his 4.97 ERA since May 17. Philly's Cristopher Sanchez has an even worse BABIP than Skenes (.337 to .310), but he has still managed a 2.52 ERA.

Aaron Judge, New York Yankees (9.7 WAR to 1.9)

Primary cause: Injury

After back-to-back 50-homer seasons and MVP awards, Judge's rib injury has led to a distressed Yankees offense that is on pace to score 114 fewer runs than in 2025. Since June 1, without Judge, the Yankees are 25th in the majors in runs scored -- although Yankees right fielders are actually seventh in the majors in OPS since that date. That suggests the offensive problems haven't so much been an inability to replace Judge, but a result of declines from other players as well, such as Austin Wells, Trent Grisham and Jazz Chisholm Jr.

Garrett Crochet, Boston Red Sox (6.0 WAR to -0.5 WAR)

Primary cause: Injury

This has perhaps been the biggest injury of the entire season, as Crochet went down after six starts with a 6.30 ERA -- and yet the Red Sox have managed pretty well without him. They are just outside the top 10 in rotation ERA, but after bottoming out at 29-43 on June 18, the Red Sox have the best record in the majors and the rotation is just outside the top five in ERA. Offseason acquisition Sonny Gray has led the way, going 16-4 with a 2.82 ERA, while rookies Payton Tolle, Jake Bennett and Connelly Early (before he was traded) have all posted ERAs under 3.50.

Trea Turner, Philadelphia Phillies (5.4 WAR to -0.5)

Primary cause: Batting average down against fastballs; terrible defensive metrics due to lack of range; career-low BABIP compared to lifetime mark.

Turner won the NL batting title last year with a .304 mark and also posted much-improved defensive metrics after rating poorly in 2023 and 2024. This year: He's hitting a lackluster .239/.292/.376 and his defense has been noticeably worse again. He ranks in the fourth percentile of Statcast's outs above average and is last among all shortstops with minus-14 defensive runs saved. The Phillies have allowed a .308 average on balls in play, with only the Athletics and Colorado Rockies worse in that department, and Turner's lack of range is a big part of that. The Phillies will make the playoffs barring a September collapse, but a better Turner would have them neck-and-neck with the Atlanta Braves in the division instead of four games behind.

Juan Soto (6.1 WAR to 2.8), New York Mets

Primary cause: Injury

Francisco Lindor (5.8 WA to 1.3), New York Mets

Primary cause: Injury and performance (suffered a calf injury in April); worst defensive metrics of his career; hitting just .211 against fastballs; struggles against left-handers

Injuries are the big factor here, as Soto has played in 89 games and Lindor 83. Soto has been excellent at the plate when he has played, but Lindor has his worst numbers since his difficult first season with the Mets in 2021. He'll be 33 next season, so there will be concerns heading into 2027 about whether he can still be an elite top-10, MVP-type player. As for the Mets, even a healthy Soto and Lindor wouldn't have saved this disaster of a season.

Jose Ramirez, Cleveland Guardians (5.9 WAR to 2.2)

Primary cause: Probably the injury (but age could also be a factor).

Ramirez has been so consistent for so long -- a top-10 MVP finish in eight of the previous nine seasons -- that it seemed like he would just roll along forever. He fractured his hamate bone on June 13 and missed a month, and he has a .651 OPS since returning. He's 33 now, and his numbers were also down before the injury (.757 OPS), so his season is difficult to assess. From June 14 to July 21, without Ramirez, the Guardians went 15-15 with a .691 OPS, right at their season OPS total of .686, so missing Ramirez didn't have a big impact on the AL Central race.

Tarik Skubal, Detroit Tigers/Los Angeles Dodgers (6.4 WAR to 3.5)

Primary cause: Injury

Well, maybe Skubal's injury will prove to be the biggest of 2026 -- especially if he helps the Dodgers win another World Series. He missed over a month of action, April 30 to June 12, after elbow surgery, and the Tigers went 14-25 when he was on the injured list. The Tigers were 6½ games out of first place on Aug. 1 when they agreed to trade Skubal, and 3½ out of the wild card. If Skubal hadn't missed that time and the Tigers won two or three of the starts he missed, maybe they would have been close enough in the race that they would have keep Skubal (and Casey Mize). Maybe.

stories.headline: Liverpool sign Djylian N'Guessan, 18, for next season
stories.summary: Liverpool have signed teenage forward Djylian N'Guessan although he won't play for the club until at least next season.
stories.body:
Liverpool have signed teenage forward Djylian N'Guessan although he won't play for the club until at least next season.

The 18-year-old will sign for Liverpool on a permanent deal in January from Saint-Etienne, but will spend this campaign on loan at Stade Brestois.

After debuting in January 2025 for Saint-Etienne, the French forward played 13 times and scored once.

N'Guessan played seven times for France in the 2025 Under-20 World Cup. Last summer he was named in the Team of the Tournament at the U17 European Championship, having scored four goals for France.

Similarly, Liverpool also wrapped up the £30 million ($41m) signing of goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans who will spend this season away on loan.

Brughmans, also 18, has signed from Belgian side KRC Genk where he will remain on-loan for this campaign.

stories.headline: Federico Chiesa left out of Liverpool's Champions League squad
stories.summary: Federico Chiesa has been left out of the squad sheet submitted by Liverpool for this year's UEFA Champions League league phase.
stories.body:
Federico Chiesa has been left out of Liverpool's squad for the league phase of the 2026-27 Champions League.

The Italy international is joined by Wataru Endo among those omitted by new boss Andoni Iraola.

Liverpool confirmed their squad ahead of the start of their European campaign against Atlético Madrid at Anfield on Sept. 9.

Both players will be unavailable for the league phase unless Liverpool are able to make a permitted change to their squad, normally injury related.

UEFA rules limit sides to a 25-player List A, with eight places reserved for 'locally trained' players, of which four must have been at the club for three seasons between the ages of 15 and 21.

Younger players can be registered separately on List B if they meet UEFA's age and development requirements, but Chiesa and Endo are not eligible.

The 28-year-old misses out with summer arrival Víctor Muñoz included, alongside Conor Bradley, who is continuing his rehabilitation from a knee injury in February. Giovanni Leoni, who suffered an ACL tear in September 2025, is also on the list.

Chiesa is currently out with a muscle injury, though a long-term absence is not expected.

Endo made only eight Premier League appearances in 2025-26, seven of them from the bench, while he featured just once in Liverpool's run to the Champions League quarterfinals.

They will travel to face Austrian side LASK, Fenerbahce, Club Brugge and Inter Milan.

Liverpool have instead included injured forward Hugo Ekitike in their squad despite the Frenchman currently being sidelined.

As expected, Ekitike's compatriot Bradley Barcola is on the list after his move from Paris Saint-Germain, worth up to £123 million ($166 million).

stories.headline: Nigeria's D'Tigress at the 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup - Everything You Need to Know
stories.summary: Nigeria's D'Tigress head to the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin as a team with an unusual combination of tournament experience and World Cup unfamiliarity.
stories.body:
Nigeria's D'Tigress head to the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin as a team with an unusual combination of global tournament experience and World Cup unfamiliarity.

Nigeria arrive as five-time defending African champions and the No. 8-ranked team in the FIBA world rankings, looking to improve on their best World Cup finish, an eighth-place showing in 2018.

The expanded 16-team World Cup runs from September 4 through13, with Nigeria drawn in Group B alongside France, South Korea and Hungary.

Here is everything you need to know about D'Tigress in Berlin.

How they qualified
Nigeria booked their place in Berlin by winning the 2025 FIBA Women's AfroBasket in Abidjan, defeating Mali 78-64 in the final to claim a fifth consecutive continental championship.

No country had previously won five consecutive Women's AfroBasket titles, and Nigeria's victory extended an unbeaten run in the competition that dates to 2015. D'Tigress have now won 29 consecutive AfroBasket games.

Ezinne Kalu led Nigeria with 20 points in the final, while Portland fire's Amy Okonkwo scored 19 as D'Tigress recovered from a slow start to pull away in the second half.

Okonkwo, who averaged 14 points and six rebounds during the tournament, was named MVP for the second consecutive AfroBasket.

Nigeria subsequently competed at the World Cup qualifying tournament in Lyon-Villeurbanne in March despite already having secured qualification as African champions.

They finished 2-3, beating Colombia 70-37 and the Philippines 101-84, while losing to South Korea 77-60, France 93-86 and Germany 81-73.

Those results carry additional significance into Berlin. Two of the teams that beat Nigeria in France, South Korea and France, have been drawn in their World Cup group.

Previous World Cup appearances
For all their success in Africa, D'Tigress have relatively little World Cup history. Berlin will be only Nigeria's third appearance at the tournament, with their tournament debut coming 20 years ago in Brazil in 2006, when they lost all five games.

It took another 12 years for them to make their breakthrough. At the 2018 World Cup in Spain, D'Tigress beat Turkey 74-68 for their first victory at the competition. They followed that by beating Argentina before defeating Greece in the qualification game to become the first African team to reach the Women's World Cup quarterfinals.

Their run ended against eventual champions the United States, but their eighth-place finish remains Nigeria's best at a World Cup.

Nigeria qualified for the 2022 tournament in Australia but did not participate after the Nigerian government withdrew the country's basketball teams from international competition amid a long-running leadership dispute within the Nigeria Basketball Federation.

That means Berlin will mark D'Tigress' return to the World Cup for the first time in eight years.

African dominance to global contenders
Nigeria's status in international basketball has changed considerably since their 2018 World Cup run. D'Tigress have won every Women's AfroBasket they have entered since 2017, claiming championships in 2017, 2019, 2021, 2023 and 2025.

The biggest evidence that their dominance could translate beyond Africa came at the Paris Olympics, when they became the first African basketball team, men's or women's, to make the Olympic quarterfinals before losing to the juggernaut that is Team USA.

On the plus side, that run pushed them into the FIBA women's world top 10 for the first time and they enter Berlin ranked No. 8.

Sadly they failed to build on that when they were withdrawn from the very next Games, the 2022 tournament in Australia.

But they have come storming back and while a return to the World Cup quarterfinals would match the achievement of the 2018 team, going further would take D'Tigress into territory no African women's, or even men's team have previously reached.

The Rena Wakama effect
Nigeria's rise has become closely associated with Rena Wakama.

Wakama became the first female coach to win the Women's AfroBasket when she led Nigeria to the 2023 championship and followed it with another title in 2025.

Between those championships came Paris. Nigeria's aggressive defense became one of the stories of the Olympic tournament, with D'Tigress applying pressure across the floor, forcing turnovers and turning those mistakes into transition opportunities.

After winning her first AfroBasket in 2023, Wakama recalled the moment she realized how much resilience she had in the team.

"Against Mozambique, we were down by 10 or 12 points," she said. "I looked into their eyes, and they told me: 'Coach, we're not going to lose this game.' And they came back to win."

Wakama's preparation for Berlin has been unusual because she has had to combine the national-team job with her role as an assistant coach with the WNBA's Chicago Sky.

Earlier this year, Wakama said the qualifying tournament in France was part of a broader process of testing Nigeria against the level of opposition they will encounter at the World Cup.

"Our preparations have been intense, and this tournament here in Lyon is an important part of that process," Wakama said.

"It gives us the opportunity to test ourselves against strong competition and evaluate where we're as a team."

stories.headline: What makes Max Verstappen so good? Career, background and F1 records
stories.summary: Max Verstappen is returning to his racing roots and is facing 100 drivers in a unique event called Max vs. 100 where the Formula 1 star will attempt to overtake 100 challengers, starting from the back of the grid.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen is returning to his racing roots and is taking part in a unique event called Max vs 100 where the Formula 1 star will attempt to overtake 100 drivers, starting from the back of the grid.

The 28-year-old currently races in F1, the highest tier in motorsport. He is one of the fiercest competitors out there and is known for his aggressive driving style and fearless overtaking.

But if you have never heard of him, or want to learn more, here is everything you need to know.

- Max vs 100: F1 superstar Verstappen to race drivers in karting event - live on Disney+

Who is Max Verstappen?
Verstappen was born in Belgium to his Dutch father Jos and his Belgian mother Sophie. His father raced in F1 between 1994-2003 and had two podium finishes, while his mother competed in karts. He currently resides in Monaco.

Who does he race for?
Verstappen started racing go-karts when he was just four years old and started to compete in championships at seven.

He then made his way through the ranks winning several world and European titles in 2013. He raced just one season in Formula 3 before skipping Formula 2 and heading straight to Formula 1.

In 2015, he signed for Red Bull junior team Toro Rosso at the age of 17 before he was promoted to Red Bull a year later.

He then went on to become the youngest ever grand prix winner after taking victory at the Spanish Grand Prix and has been at Red Bull ever since, becoming the most successful driver at the team.

He signed a long-term contract back in March 2022 to stay at the Milton Keynes-based team until the end of 2028, and before the Dutch Grand Prix this year he penned a new deal keeping him at the team until 2030.

What has he achieved?
It was clear from the early days that Verstappen was going to be an exceptional racing driver and he's become a phenomenon since with a killer instinct.

He's had 244 race starts in F1 and has been on the top step of the podium 71 times. He's been on the podium 131 times and is just two pole positions away from reaching 50 career poles.

The Dutchman has four world championships which he won back-to-back in a dominant Red Bull era between 2021-2024.

He also has an impressive list of achievements to his name, one being in 2023 where he recorded the most wins [19] and the most podium finishes [21] in a single season. He also recorded 10 consecutive race victories.

When is Max vs 100?
The event is taking place on Sept. 16 and will be streamed live on Disney+.

Why is he racing in Max vs 100?

Verstappen has never been shy of getting his teeth stuck into other forms of motorsport away from Formula 1. He most recently made his debut at the iconic Nürburgring 24 Hours in May, driving a Mercedes-AMG GT3.

This will be a slightly different challenge for the Dutchman, but no doubt one he will enjoy with his competitive nature.

"In go-karts you learn all the basics: starts, defending, overtaking," Verstappen said. "Of course, I spent a long period of my life go-karting, so it's always nice to return."

The event is taking place at Silverstone in the U.K. and a circuit has been purpose-built for the occasion. It's set to be the biggest go-kart event in the world.

stories.headline: South Africa's Lyle Foster joins Dynamo on loan from Burnley
stories.summary: South Africa's Lyle Foster joined the Houston Dynamo on loan from Burnley on Thursday through summer of 2027.
stories.body:
South Africa's Lyle Foster joined the Houston Dynamo FC on loan from Burnley on Thursday through summer of 2027.

Foster, 25, spent the past four seasons with Burnley, making 89 league appearances and scoring 11 goals across Premier League and EFL Championship play.

He helped Burnley earn promotion to the Premier League twice, including winning the 2022-23 Championship title and securing automatic promotion with a second-place finish during the 2024-25 campaign.

"Lyle presents another powerful, mobile forward to our attacking group," Dynamo president of soccer Pat Onstad said in a news release. "He threatens the space behind the back line, links play well and brings the work rate and intensity that we demand without the ball. Lyle's experience in the Premier League and on the international stage will strengthen our group, and we are excited to welcome him to Houston as we prepare for a strong finish to the season."

Foster joined Burnley from K.V.C. Westerlo in January 2023 after helping the side win the Belgian second-division title and earn promotion following the 2021-22 season. He got his start with the Orlando Pirates and then joined AS Monaco in January 2019 before stints with Brugge and Vitória S.C.

Foster has earned 33 senior caps and scored 11 goals for South Africa since making his debut in 2018. He helped Bafana Bafana advance to the knockout stage at the 2026 World Cup for the first time in federation history.

Houston currently sits second in the Western Conference with 39 points and a 12-7-3 (W-L-D) record and they travel to Charlotte FC on Saturday.

stories.headline: Fantasy hockey drafts: Which player should you take with the first pick?
stories.summary: Picking first? Here are the players you should consider with the No. 1 overall pick in fantasy hockey drafts.
stories.body:
Before mining the draft for valuable sleepers, potential overachievers and breakout candidates, first you have to grab the Shohei Ohtani, Jahmyr Gibbs, Taylor Swift, if you will, of the fantasy hockey world. The megastar to drive your team bus by reliably piling up more points on the daily than anyone else.

I can't remember another season where whittling down the list of eligible candidates to go first overall was so clear-cut. While I forced myself to make positive arguments for several other players as a necessary exercise, each member of the following quartet always emerged superior. So, in loose order, here's who to draft if you're fortunate to do so early on.

Please note that each player's strength is assessed within the framework of ESPN's standard H2H points game, in step with the following formula:

Skaters:

Goals = 2 points

Assists = 1 point

Shots and Hits = 0.1 points

Blocked shots and Special-teams points = 0.5 points

More: Sign up today | Rankings | Projections | Which league is right for you?

Nathan MacKinnon, F, Colorado Avalanche
I'll keep this short because his numbers are superlatively sweet. The Colorado center checks all relevant fantasy boxes, most with extra aplomb. Firing on net more often than anyone else for the third straight year, MacKinnon racked up 74 assists and 30 power-play points on 350 shots, while earning a sufficient number of hits and blocked shots to satisfy any demanding fantasy player. In this space last year, I suggested managers draft MacKinnon first overall and "hope he scores closer to 51 [goals] like in 2023-24." Well, he rifled home 53. Only Connor McDavid equaled MacKinnon in averaging 3.2 fantasy points per game in ESPN's standard fantasy league.

So, once more with feeling: Draft him first overall and hope he scores near 53 like last year. A total of 45 or so would also feel digestible enough.

Nikita Kucherov, F, Tampa Bay Lightning

Bit more to say here. A few weeks after securing his arguably overdue second Hart Trophy, the league's ultimate playmaker is once more ready to set the fantasy hockey world alight. No regular skater averaged more points per game (1.71) than Kucherov in 2025-26, not even that fella in Edmonton who flirted with the 140 total points mark. Exceptional terrain the elite winger might've reached himself had he not missed six games.

Never mind Kucherov doesn't fire on net as much as MacKinnon or Connor McDavid or bolster other nonscoring fantasy categories in any significant way. It's all about the production with this guy, and not just assists. In addition to providing 86 helpers this past run, he also has 44 goals to show for 76 contests. All the while delivering his fortunate managers with an average of 3.1 fantasy points/game, sharing rarefied air with only MacKinnon and McDavid in the 3.0-plus club. No reason to believe we're not in for similar numbers in 2026-27.

Plus, the 33-year-old is reliable enough nowadays. Since missing the entire 2020-21 regular season -- before, ahem, winning his second Stanley Cup a few weeks later -- then half a campaign to follow, Kucherov is serving as remarkably durable. There isn't a fantasy manager on the planet who's going to gripe about any player missing only 11 total games through four seasons. Especially when they're banging out 1.68 points/game three calendars running. Oh, and guess who's entering a contract year with the salary cap skyrocketing? Right. Even the fiercest competitors on the planet aren't immune to such extra incentivization. After MacKinnon, the Lightning star is my top fantasy pick.

Justification for selecting Kucherov first overall: His prospective power-play production. Last year's "measly" haul of 37 points with the extra skater falls well short of totals from previous seasons. Then there's the rather significant gap in quality between Tampa Bay's top unit and its second. Projecting that the elite winger sees a lot of time with the man-advantage and positively regresses back to his personal mean -- 50 power-play points through three previous campaigns -- could rationalize picking him first overall.

Macklin Celebrini, F, San Jose Sharks

It's all about the ceiling with this young man. After erupting for 45 goals and 70 assists in his second NHL season and more than holding his own at the Olympics as a teenager, Celebrini is just getting going. Growing up together with teammates Will Smith (21), Michael Misa (19) and Igor Chernyshov (20), the Ted Lindsay Award finalist is expected to take another step forward as a bigger and stronger player, equally if not bettering, his outstanding sophomore numbers. For starters, don't be surprised if he shoots more often on net, eclipsing the 300-shot mark for the first time. Proud of his 200-foot game, Celebrini could also conceivably improve on last year's total of 53 blocked shots. Those half-points add up fast.

The one fantasy concern lies in the goal-scoring department. Owning a 15.7% shooting percentage and, according to Evolving Hockey, an expected goals rate of 35 ixG, the Sharks center found the back of the net 45 times. Bit of a chasm there. Either Celebrini is just that much better, and therefore more accurate (completely plausible), or some good fortune was in play. My point is that this is why some models project Celebrini to bank approximately 40 goals -- and not 50 -- in 2026-27. Still, the lad's potential is too ripe to disregard. I'm grabbing him without hesitation, once McKinnon and Kucherov are off the board.

Justification for selecting Celebrini first overall: The Ivar Stenberg factor. Coach Ryan Warsovsky now has another option to toss alongside Celebrini at even strength and on the power play. Maybe the 2026 second overall draft pick serves as a delightful fit that brings even more out of the burgeoning superstar. If not, Warsofsky has many other talented and maturing options, even with William Eklund gone for Ottawa.

Connor McDavid, F, Edmonton Oilers

I know what you're thinking: What fantasy manager in their right mind would bypass the best player in our known universe with the second or, my goodness, third draft pick in any conventional league. I get the bewilderment, but hear me out. First of all, this teeny slide is less a knock on McDavid himself and more a reflection of the three preceding names and their dynamite potential in 2026-27.

Then there's the Oilers' power play to think about. Leading the league with a success rate of 30.6%, Edmonton's special teams unit will be hard-pressed to replicate that outstanding figure. Which means McDavid can't again count on nearing a tally of 54 points with the extra skater. Of course he makes Edmonton's unit better. Still, another 54-plus is a big ask for a player who has averaged about half a power-play point per game in his career, including the ridiculous Mario Lemieux-esque haul of 71 in 2021-22.

Another fantasy concern is the influence of the new guy behind the bench. Recognized for his commitment to greater defensive accountability and balancing lines and ice time, Mike Babcock isn't a fan of wild, open offensive play. Of course, he's still going to let McDavid cook, but more likely with the gas turned up to eight instead of 10. This is the coach both the megastar center and Leon Draisaitl wanted. While they won't give a lick about reduced personal numbers if it leads to a Cup, fantasy managers should still slightly temper their expectations.

Justification for selecting McDavid first overall: Because he's Connor McDavid, that's why. In the face of each logic-driven and exceptionally rational argument above, he could still magically score 140 points in 84 healthy games.

stories.headline: Song Yadong KO's Umar Nurmagomedov in massive UFC upset
stories.summary: Song Yadong pulled off a massive upset by knocking out heavily favored Umar Nurmagomedov in the men's bantamweight main event of UFC Fight Night in Shanghai.
stories.body:
Song Yadong saved the greatest performance of his career for his home country, knocking out former title challenger Umar Nurmagomedov in the men's bantamweight main event of UFC Fight Night on Saturday in Shanghai.

Song (24-9-1, 1 NC), a nearly 5-1 underdog at DraftKings Sportsbook, dropped Nurmagomedov with a short right hand, drawing a roar from the crowd when the fight was waved off at 1 minute, 48 seconds of Round 2.

"I believe in myself, and my team believed that I would win this fight," Song said through an interpreter. "They told me I would knock this guy out, and I did it."

It was the second straight fight in China for Song and his second straight win by finish. His most recent knockout win had been in 2023.

Song, making his first appearance in Shanghai since his UFC debut at age 19 in 2017, walked out to a hero's welcome.

"Nine years ago, I wanted to show I could walk in this Octagon," he said. "Nine years later, I want to prove I am the best in the world. I am the best Chinese fighter in the world."

The knockout came after Nurmagomedov (20-2) ducked out of the way of a left hand and right into the path of a short right hand, which connected near his right ear and sent him limply to the canvas. Song delivered three finishing shots on the mat before the referee jumped in.

That sent Song running around inside the cage in celebration, where he nearly ran into Nurmagomedov's younger brother and cornerman, PFL lightweight champion Usman Nurmagomedov, who had rushed in to check on his fallen brother. Usman Nurmagomedov appeared to throw an elbow in Song's direction as the elated winner was running past.

Song climbed atop the cage to soak in the fans' cheers before jumping down outside the cage and running into the crowd to get hugs and high-fives from fans.

"Maybe not today, maybe not tomorrow, maybe not next month, but I will be the first male Chinese UFC champion," Song said through the interpreter, with the "male" designation a nod to countrywoman Zhang Weili, a two-time women's champion at strawweight.

Song, who trains in Sacramento, California, switched to English and yelled, "Give me the title shot!"

stories.headline: Blame the coach: Tale of two disastrous seasons
stories.summary: Fairly or unfairly, the spotlight is on the coaches of the Bulldogs and Broncos after two very different but equally awful seasons.
stories.body:
In front of an expectedly dismal crowd, two of the NRL's biggest clubs met for the last game of their miserable 2026 seasons. Those willing to fork out a minimum $45 for a general admission ticket to the cavernous Accor Stadium were treated to a mistake-riddled first half, with the Bulldogs squandering a majority of possession and being a man up for 10 minutes to go to the break locked at 10-10.

The Bulldogs' best passage of play for the entire night came in the 34th minute, with a move they had obviously been saving up for this meaningless occasion. Starting inside the Broncos' 20, the ball was passed from Jake Turpin at dummy-half to Bailey Hayward at first receiver, to Lachie Galvin at halfback to Viliame Kikau, who turned his back to pass to Stephen Crichton at five-eighth who doubled around before cutting out centre Bronson Xerri to find Enari Tuala who crossed in the corner.

The one movement summed up all that has been wrong at the Bulldogs in 2026. Turpin came on to play dummy-half, and instead of replacing Hayward he pushed him to first receiver, a role he was sharing with Jaeman Salmon at the time. This in turn pushed Galvin to second receiver, where he is at his best in the five-eighth position. Crichton and Xerri were then left to fight over the decoy runner role, otherwise you would have two centres on that side of the field. It's a complete mess and only worked on this one occasion, in a move not seen before nor since.

Coach Cameron Ciraldo has tried his best through 2026 to make the most of the players at his disposal. The Bulldogs lack quality spine players, but Ciraldo has compounded the problem by selecting those he does have out of position. On top of that he has them playing a game plan that brings out the worst in all of them.

Hayward is a half playing at dummy-half, he stands up to pass, his passes are looping and often inaccurate and he poses no real run threat. Early in games Ciraldo has him passing to Salmon who then distributes it with the opposition defence all over him.

Salmon has been playing some career-best football of late, but you still wouldn't have him in a list of the 10 best No. 13s in the League. You certainly wouldn't have him anywhere near a list of ball-playing forwards, and yet week after week Ciraldo has him at first receiver for large parts of the game. He consistently manages to kill off any momentum the Bulldogs may have acquired.

At fullback Connor Tracey forms another part of the dysfunctional spine. If everyone played with his heart the Bulldogs would be a better side, but his handling, nerve under the high ball and attacking prowess leave him a long way short of the attacking weapon the good teams have in that position.

Into the second half, the Broncos found some spark, and began carving up a disinterested Bulldogs defence on the back of characteristic errors.

Crichton, easily one of the best centres in the game, has been moved into the halves by Ciraldo. He has clearly floundered, exposing a poor passing and kicking game, while strangling his greatest asset, his ability to cause havoc when running on the edge. As the Bulldogs fell apart in the second half, he threw a 10-metre spiral pass so poorly timed and directed that it fell into the arms of a Broncos defender who very nearly set up another try.

The Bulldogs were being thumped by a team struggling at the bottom of the ladder, a team which had inexplicably plunged from premiers to no-hopers in the space of a year. Where had it all gone wrong for the Broncos?

They had only really lost Selwyn Cobbo at the end of 2025, while adding depth players in Grant Anderson from the Storm and Tom Duffy from the Cowboys. Sure Adam Reynolds and Ben Hunt were a year older, and wearier, but still capable. Reece Walsh had his share of injuries through the season and front-row talisman Payne Haas had thrown a spanner in the works by announcing that he was leaving for the Rabbitohs in 2027. From a roster perspective there weren't any legitimate excuses for such a dramatic fall.

Rumours circulated that coach Michael Maguire had lost the dressing room. Players were muttering that his methods were too hard, the preseason brutal, egos were bruised, players pushed beyond exhaustion. The morale splintered, the belief in what they were being asked to do waned. Which, to any reasonable outsider would seem completely incomprehensible.

Maguire's methods had brought the club its first premiership in 19 years. The players were covered in glory, the city of Brisbane rejoiced, and now it was all too hard? Did they somehow think the Panthers won four straight titles by taking it easier after winning the first one?

Maguire is a proven winner, with a State of Origin series in his one attempt, two NRL premierships and one Super League title to his name. But, the Broncos aren't the only team to ultimately reject Maguire's methods. At the Rabbitohs he went from a peak win percentage in his second season of 72% to a low of 37% in his final year. At the Tigers he squeezed a 45% win rate out of the perennial strugglers, which dipped to 25% in his final year. His first year at the Broncos brought a premiership with a 65% win rate, which plummeted to 31% this year.

Aren't these players well-paid to do what the coach demands of them? Is it the ultimate display of a chasm between generations? A coach from a harder, more straight forward era, pushing a generation less likely to respond to harsh words or sustain a high level of physical exertion for any prolonged period of time. Success for this generation is often measured in the size of the pay packet, and that arrives regardless of results. Not happy with the coach's methods? Back off your effort a fraction and soon enough he'll be the one shown the door.

The Broncos showed that when committed to the cause, they still have the talent to put on plenty of tries and contain an attack as disjointed as the Bulldogs.

With four minutes remaining in the game, and the Broncos leading 35-20, the Bulldogs played the ball five metres out. Hayward picked it up took a step and a half to his right, and by the time he threw his looping pass to Jacob Preston he was already into the defensive line. The ball hit him on the backside and the Broncos dived on it.

It was a moment that encapsulated a frustrating Bulldogs season in a loss to a Broncos team which really let itself and its fans down.
